### page_15
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
A systematic palaeomagnetic/rock magnetic investigation, involving detailed
palaeomagnetic and petrophysical analysis of 578 oriented samples, was carried out on
the late Archaean to Palaeo proterozoic rock formations and in-situ iron deposits in the
Hamersley Province. Five phases of magnetic remanence have been identified.
(1) A steep-downward remanence from little-deformed Fortescue Group volcaniclastic
rocks that is directed to the south-east. This remanence, revealed from four
sampling sites only, is possibly of primary origin.
(2) A steep-downward magnetic overprint directed to the south-west. This remanence is
commonly carried by hematite and martite. It is younger than the E-W trending
folds related to the Ophthalmian deformation «2450 to -2200 Ma) and older than
ENE-trending folds related to the Mt Whale back Fault. The remanence is pervasive
in the Newman, West Angelas and Area C regions (including all studied ore bodies in
those regions). but becomes less prominent in the Tom Price and Paraburdoo
regions, and is absent in the western (Duck Creek region) and northern (Hamersley
and Chichester Ranges) Hamersley Province. It is interpreted to be of
thermal/chemical (mostly chemical) origin, possibly acquired at the end of the
Ophthalmia Orogeny (ca. 2200 Ma). A possible alternative is that the magnetisation
was acquired during the late stage of the Ashburton Orogeny (ca. 1800-1650 Ma).
(3) A shallow to moderately inclined magnetic overprint directed upward to the north
west. It was acquired either toward the late stage of, or after, the NW -trending
folding related to the Ashburton Orogeny (between ca. 1800 Ma and 1650 Ma). The
remanence is widespread in the western, central and northern Hamersley Province
(including the Barrett-Lennard, Paraburdoo, Channar, and Tom Price deposits). but
less prominent in the eastern Hamersley Province. It is the only remanence found in
the Barrett-Lennard deposit and the M-(mpl h) ores in the Channar deposit. It
appears to be of mostly chemical origin in iron ores and SIFs, of thermal/ chemical
origin in carbonate (where this overprint is pervasive), and mostly of thermal origin in
volcanic rocks. The temperature causing the thermal overprint in some of the
volcanic rocks is estimated to be ca. 250 ± 100'C. It is believed to be related to fluids
driven by the Ashburton Orogeny, or possibly could be a little younger.
(4) A preliminary remanent direction (shallow downward to NNE) from five samples of
baked rocks in, and around, a NE-trending dolerite dyke in Channar Mine, gives a
pole position close to that of the 755 ± 3 Ma Mundine Well dyke swarm in the
Pilbara.
(5) Mostly Cenozoic overprints reflecting either weathering or viscous remanent
magnetisation. Whereas overprints of weathering origin are normally carried by
1

### page_16
hematite, and in some places by maghemite and goethite, the viscous remanence is
normally carried by magnetite.
Our palaeomagnetic results suggest two major phases of martite-microplaty
hematite formation or recrystallisation, and thus iron ore magnetisation, in the
Hamersley Province. The first corresponds to the steep southwest-directed regional
remagnetisation, and could have occurred late during, or after, the Ophthalmia Orogeny
(ca. 2400 to 2200 Ma). An alternative interpretation is that it could have formed during
the 1800-1650 Ma Ashburton Orogeny. This event was important for hematite/martite
ore formation in both the eastern (Mt Whaleback, Ore Bodies 23 and 25, Area C) and
central (Tom Price and Paraburdoo deposits) Hamersley Province, but there is no sign of
it in the western Hamersley Province (i.e., the Barrett-Lennard deposit and the M-(mpl
h) ores in Channar deposit). The second phase, most likely related to the Ashburton
Orogeny (ca. 1800 to 1650 Mal, is dominant in the western-central Hamersley Province
(Barrett-Lennard and Channar deposits), and it strongly reworked the iron deposits in
central Hamersley Province (Tom Price and Paraburdoo deposits), but had little impact
on the deposits in eastern Hamersley Province (Mt Whaleback, Ore Bodies 23 and 25,
and Area C deposits). We thus see a mixed, but dominantly the younger, magnetic
overprint in the central Hamersley Province deposits.
Palaeomagnetic results further suggest that the first phase of ore genesis (ca. 2200 Ma)
occurred when the Pilbara was at a palaeolatitude of ca. 50', whereas the second
(possibly minor) phase (ca. 1700 Ma) occurred at a tropical palaeolatitude. We have
also established a comprehensive petrophysical database for the Hamersley Province
rock units and iron deposits during the course of this project.
The ca. 755 Ma NE-trending dyke intrusions caused localised magnetite mineralisation
only (i.e., the small magnetite ore bodies in contact with a NE-trending dyke in the
Channar Mine). We see no evidence for any Mesozoic to Tertiary mineralisation in the
in-situ deposits apart from the formation of a surface hard cap.
In terms of ore genesis for the in-situ iron ore deposits in the Hamersley Province, our
results do not support the supergene model in the following aspects:
(1) Results of this study indicate that mineralisation is related to widespread thermal
chemical events at a variety of stratigraphic, structural and geomorphological levels.
Magnetic overprints related to the second mineralisation event (ca. 1700 Ma?) spread
as far north as the Chichester Range. The supergene model has difficulties in
2

### page_17
explaining the widespread and pervasive thermal/chemical overprint which is found
in the non-BIF rocks in the northern Hamersley Province as well as in the
mineralised zones. Such widespread thermal-chemical events can be readily
explained by tectonic/thermal fluid flow related either to orogenic and/or magmatic
activity.
(2) We see no evidence of martite formed by Mesozoic/Tertiary supergene processes.
Instead, palaeomagnetic results suggest that the M-((g)) or M-(( )) ores in the eastern
Hamersley Basin (Orebody 25 and Area C deposits) were formed during the
MNI/HPI mineralisation event that formed the M-(mpl h) ores (e.g., Mt Whaleback).
Microplaty hematite and martite probably represent different levels of oxidation and
recrystallisation, and coexist in the same deposit because of the variations in the
physical-chemical conditions. The relatively small amount of goethite (compared
with martite/hematite) in some deposits is attributed to Mesozoic to Recent
weathering.
(3) The presence of large hematite crystals in the matrix of hematite conglomerate in
both the Barrett-Lennard deposit and the basal Wyloo Group, as well as in veins in
sandstones of the upper Wyloo Group, clearly suggests a hypogene origin. Hematite
pebbles in the Barrett-Lennard deposit carry the same remanence as authigenic
hematite in the matrix which suggests that the hematite in those pebbles was also
recrystallised during the hydrothermal process. Zones of very coarse microplaty
hematite have also been found in the Channar Main deposit. Samples from both the
Barrett-Lennard deposit and the Channar Main deposit carry a single-component
NM2/HP2 remanence only, therefore ruling out the influence of any younger event.
(4) The identification of southwesterly-sourced hematite ore grains from the basal
Beasley River Quartzite meanS that microplaty-hematite ores already existed and
were uplifted during the Ophthalmia Orogeny. This removes the possibility
suggested by Morris (1985) that the microplaty hematite ores were initially formed as
martite-goethite ores by a long period of weathering across the unconformity at the
base of the Beasley River Quartzite, and subsequently converted to microplaty
hematite by burial metamorphism below an as-yet-unidentified succession of rocks.
(5) The temporal and spatial relationship between the mineralisation and orogenic
events, and the elevated (200'C to 400'C) temperature of fluids involved, are
inconsistent with a supergene ore genesis. High-temperature mineralisation events
have also been reported by other researchers from the Tom Price deposit.
3

### page_18
However, the hypogene model has difficulty in explaining the source of the large amount
of oxygen that was required for oxidising the magnetite in the BIFs into
martite/hematite. We adopt here an hybrid ore genesis model for the martite and
microplaty-hematite deposits in the Hamersley Province. The model involves the
mixture of both hot basinal fluids and cooler meteoric fluids driven from the uplifted
mountain belt into the foreland basin. The meteoric fluids provided the crucial oxygen
needed to oxidise the original magnetite in the BIFs into martite/hematite. The model is
basically a hypogene one with elements (i.e. the involvement of meteoric fluids) from the
supergene model. Such an ore genesis model may apply to both phases of
mineralisation in the Hamersley Province.
4

### page_19
2. INTRODUCTION
2.1 AIMS OF THIS PROJECT
The M242 research proposal laid out the major aims of this project:
•... the most important thing to test is the timing and extent of the ore:genesis related
magnetic overprint. A further palaeomagnetic study is therefore proposed aiming at
the following targets:
I, To test further whether the remanence is post-folding, but pre-Mount McGrath
Formation, and to demonstrate further whether the ore bodies share the same
remanence.
2, To examine the extent of the ore-genesis related magnetic overprint, and therefore to
test the hypogene model. This will involve sampling the Hamersley Group at various
distances from the iron-ore deposits. Sampling should be carried out on magnetically
more isotropic rocks like dolomite, red shales, as well as the anisotropic BIFs.
3, To examine the age of the M-G ores by sampling some typical ore bodies, and
comparing the remanent directions in these ores with that from the M-(mpl H) type
ores.
4, As an extension of 2, palaeomagnetism of the Fortescue Group and the Wyloo
Group (particularly the latter), wherever suitable, should be systematically studied.
This will help in defining the poorly known Late Archaean to Early Proterozoic APWP
for the Pilbara craton, and therefore assist in clarifying the relative age of the Newman
deposit and the other deposits.
5, To examine whether the ore bodies have suffered any ductile strain by measuring
the magnetic fabric. This is another test for the relative age of the deposits.
6, To examine the timing relationship between the WNW (NW)-trending dolerite dyke
swarms and the ore genesis by studying the dykes palaeomagnetically both around the
ore deposits and at distance."
5

### page_20
2.2 REGIONAL GEOLOGY
The Hamersley Province is located on the southern Pilbara Craton of Western Australia.
It is characterised by a succession of low-grade metamorphic, late Archaean to early
Palaeo proterozoic volcanic rocks, banded iron-formations (BIFs), carbonates and clastic
rocks overlying an Archaean granite and greenstone basement (Fig. 2.1). The basal
succession of the Mount Bruce Supergroup, the Fortescue Group, consists mainly of
basalts with some felsic volcanic rocks and sandstones, possibly formed in a rift
environment (e.g., Blake and Barley, 1992).
The ca. 2500-m thick Hamersley Group consists of five major BIF units, a thick
dolomite unit, shales, mafic volcanic rocks and dolerite sills (Fig. 2.2) (e.g., Macleod,
1966; Trendall, 1983). A notable feature of the iron-formations is the lateral continuity
of each unit throughout the Hamersley Province with no apparent facies change within
them. The Hamersley Group is conformably overlain by the Turee Creek Group, which
consists of arenite, wacke, mudstone, carbonate and minor basalt. Unconformably
overlying the Turee Creek Group are the Wyloo Group clastic rocks, dolomite, basalts
and volcanic rocks.
The Hamersley Group is traditionally regarded as having been deposited on a stable
marine platform (e.g. Morris and Horwitz, 1983; Tyler and Thorne, 1990). Blake and
Barley (1992) interpreted the lower Hamersley Group as deposits on a passive cratonic
margin, and the upper Hamersley Group as deposits in a back-arc platformal setting.
The Turee Creek Group has previously been interpreted as deposits on a passive
continental margin of the southern Pilbara Craton (e.g. Tyler and Thorne, 1990).
However, recent basin studies in the region suggest that the uppermost Hamersley
Group, the Turee Creek Group and lower Wyloo Group represent deposits in a foreland
basin (the McGrath Trough of Horwitz, 1983, 1990), with sediments derived dominantly
from the foreland fold-and-thrust belt to its south and southwest (the Ophthalmia Fold
Belt) (Horwitz and Powell, 1992; Powell and Horwitz, 1994; Martin et al., 1999). This
foreland basin, and related fold-and-thrust belt, developed after accumulation of the
2449 ± 3 Ma Woongarra Rhyolite (Barley et al., 1997) of the Hamersley Group, and
persisted until accumulation of the lower part of the Cheela Springs Basalt of the lower
Wyloo Group (2209 ± 15 Ma, SHRIMP U-Pb, Martin et al., 1998).
The Hamersley Province underwent two major phases of shortening deformation during
the Proterozoic (Figs 2.2 and 2.3), the first being the ca. 2400 to 2200 Ma Ophthalmia

Figure 2.3 A schematic tectonic history of the Hamersley Province.
A. Representation of the geology after deposition of the Weeli Woill Formation and
associated Woongarra Rhyolite. The Hamersley Province is shown as underlain by the
older (3500 to 2900 Ma) Archaean granite-greenstone, now extensively exposed in the
northern Pilbara, and also in the Rocklea and Milli Milli Domes in the southern
Hamersley Province. The overlying Fortescue Group was laid down during active
extension in terrestrial to marine conditions, which accounts for the greater thickness
preserved in the southern part of the Province. A possible ESE-trending graben is
shown in the southern part of the Province. The overlying Hamersley Group is an
alternation of banded iron-formations (BIFs), dolomitic shale and dolerite sills, the BIFs
being remarkable in their lateral continuity and maintenance of uniform thickness
across the Hamersley Province.
S. Representation of the geology after deposition of the Turee Creek Group, before the
onset of extension related to the formation of the Ashburton Trough. The McGrath
Trough, a foreland basin in front of the northward-advancing Ophthalmia fold-and
thrust belt, is thickest and coarsest-grained on the southern margin of the Hamersley
Province, and wedges out to shale and iron formation to the north.
C. The structural geometry after emplacement of the foreland fold-and-thrust belt, with
circled numbers indicating the following structures: 1. Basement thrust over Mt Bruce
Supergroup (e.g., Sylvania Inlier, south of Newman); 2. Basement involvement in cover
9

### page_24
folding, implying detachment within the basement (e.g., Rocklea Dome, western
Hamersley Province); 3. Thrust fault breaching an anticline (e.g., structures north of
Newman); 4. Blind thrust in core of an anticline (e.g., inferred structure for much of the
northern part of the Ophthalmia fold-and-thrust belt); 5. Tip line of cover detachment at
northern limit of fold-and-thrust belt (e.g., expected structure along the Hamersley
Ranges).
Based on work by Trendall and Blockley (1970), Morris and Horwitz (1983),
Harmsworth et at. (1990); Horwitz (1990), Tyler and Thorne (1990), Blake and Barley
(1992), Barley et.a!' (1997), Blake (1993), Powell and Horwitz (1994), Martin et al.
(1998, 1999), Powell et al. (1999), Tyler and Thorne (1990), Tyler (1990, 1991), Tyler et
al. (1990, 1992), and references in the published works.
Orogeny. Folds formed by this orogeny are generally ductile in style (Fig. 2.4), with axes
trending between 80° and 110°. These folds are commonly called F, in the Hamersley
Province, and this terminology is followed throughout this report. The Ophthalmia
Orogeny was the strongest along the southern margin of the Hamersley Province, and
dies out toward the northern Hamersley province (Fig. 2.5). A flood basalt, the Cheela
Springs Basalt, was emplaced before the final stage of the Ophthalmia folding, around
2200 Ma (Dow et al., 1997). A series of NW -trending dolerite dykes that cut the main F,
folds are arguably the feeders to the Cheela Springs Basalt.
The other orogenic event in the region was the Ashburton Orogeny, which occurred
between ca. 1800 and 1650 Ma. This orogeny was strongest along the southwestern
margin of the Hamersley Province, where a series of northwesterly-trending folds and
faults truncate the earlier E-trending structures (Figure 2.6). The extent of deformation
related to this orogeny in the eastern Hamersley Province is not clear. In this report we
follow the convention of calling the Ashburton Orogeny-related folding F,.
A period of extension occurred between the two orogenies after deposition of the lower
Cheela Springs Basalt, during which the 1843 Ma June Hills Volcanics and lower
Ashburton Formation accumulated. Low-angle normal faults that truncate F, folds and
are folded by F, and F. folds are found in the iron ore mines (Ronaszeki et al., 1995) and
could have formed during the extension. A more detailed discussion about the tectonic
evolution of the region is given in Chapter 3.

2.3 IRON DEPOSITS IN THE HAMERSLEY PROVINCE AND ORE GENESIS MODELS
The Hamersley Province of Western Australia (WA) hosts some of the world's largest
high-grade iron deposits, i.e., the Mt. Whaleback deposit at Newman (BHP), the Tom
Price, Paraburdoo, Marandoo and Channar deposits (Hamersley Iron Pty Ltd), the West
Angelas deposits (Robe River Mining Associates), and the Hope Downs deposit (Hancock
Prospecting Pty Ltd). In addition, there are significant Tertiary channel iron deposits
(e.g., the BHP Iron Ore Yandi deposit east of Wittenoom, and the Robe River deposit of
Robe River Iron Associates at Pannawonica). The region has a known " ... total high
grade reserve of about 20 billion tonnes of less than 0.08% P [which] rises to over 30
billion tonnes if the phosphorous constraint is removed" (Townsend and Flint, 1997).
The ore bodies with current economic importance can be subdivided into four major
types (Morris, 1985):
1. Martite-micropiaty hematite-goethite ores. This is the highest quality, and
economically most important, are type in the region. The best known ore bodies of this
type include the Mt. Whaleback, Tom Price, Paraburdoo and Channar ore bodies (e.g.,
Harmsworth et al., 1990, p. 635). The appearance of the ores varies from hard (lumpy)
ores, to soft ores and dust ores (e.g. Morris, 1985; Harmsworth et al., 1990). All the
major martite-microplaty hematite ore bodies are located in synclines along the strongly
12

### page_27
folded and faulted southern part of the Hamersley Province (e.g. Morris, 1985;
Harmsworth et aI., 1990; Tyler, 1991), indicating possible genetic relationships between
the ore genesis and structure.
2. Martite-goethite ores. This type of ore consists mainly of martite and goethite, with
little or no microplaty hematite. It is thought to be related to the Mesozoic
palaeosurface (e.g., Harmsworth et al., 1990), and occurs mostly in structurally less
complex places, such as the Section 6 deposit of the Tom Price Mine, and the Marandoo
Mine, 35 Jan northeast of Tom Price.
3. Goethite-rich channel-related deposits (so-called 'pisolites') (Harmsworth et aI., 1990,
p. 617). The best example of this ore type is the Robe River deposit at Pannawonica,
which is clearly related to the Mesozoic or younger drainage system.
4. Detrital ores, including ore conglomerates, eluvial ·scree ores' and ·canga". This ore
type is related to mid-Cenozoic weathering of the older "Tertiary surface" of the
Hamersley Province. A typical ore body of this type is the Brockman 2 deposit (D.
Kepert, 29 November 1999 email comments).
Ore Genesis Models for the Martite-microplaty Hematite Deposits
The pisolitic channel-related and detrital types of iron deposits were both formed on (or
near) erosional surfaces, and their ages can be roughly constrained by their
stratigraphic positions. It is the timing and ore genesis of the first two types of deposits,
which have the highest economic importance, that are still open to interpretation.
Two types of genetic model have been proposed for the in situ enriched hematite ores in
the Hamersley Province: hypogene and supergene (see reviews by Morris, 1986). A third
possible model, the syngenetic model, has not formally been proposed for deposits in
the region, and will not be discussed further in this report.
The hypogene model was first introduced to the Hamersley iron deposits by Neilson
(1965) following Brazilian work by Dorr (1965). Neilson (1965) suggested that the
mineralisation was due to the circulation of hydrothermal solutions during the
Palaeoproterozoic, possibly related to magmatic activities. A similar model was adopted
by Kneeshaw in 1975 (Kneeshaw, 1975). but has since been largely ignored until the
1990s.
13

### page_28
The supergene model, first proposed by MacLeod et al. (1963), suggests that these ores
were associated with either present or past weathering surfaces. This has been the
dominant view for the past thirty years, particularly since the research work by Morris
and colleagues started in 1976 (e.g. Morris, 1985, 1986; Harmsworth et al., 1990). In
Morris et al.'s model, the iron enrichment occurred during a weathering process after
the BIFs were folded. The initial martite-goethite ores were then converted to microplaty
hematite ores during burial metamorphism. The timing of the mineralisation is
constrained by geological observations that no ore-grade pebbles had been found in the
Beasley River Quartzite, but platy hematite ore pebbles appear in the younger Mount
McGrath Formation (Morris, 1980, 1985). They considered the second type of in situ
enriched ores (the martite-goethite type) to have formed dominantly during the
Mesozoic-Tertiary erosion of the Hamersley Province. A schematic diagram illustrating
the Morris et al.'s supergene model is given in Figure 2.7.
Revision of the Ore Genesis Models for the Martite-microplaty Hematite Deposits
There has been some rethinking of the ore genesis models in recent years by both
academic and company geologists. Li et al. (1993) questioned the supergene model for
the martite-microplaty hematite deposits on both geological and geophysical grounds.
Through reinterpretation of previous palaeomagnetic results, particularly those by Clark
and Schmidt (1986) and Schmidt and Clark (1994). and with their own results from a
preliminary study in the region, they suggested that there was probably a regional
thermal/chemical event in at least the southern Hamersley Province after the formation
of the E-trending F, folds related to the early Palaeoproterozoic Ophthalmia Orogeny,
which led to the formation of hypogene microplaty hematite deposits. This revised
hypogene model suggested that the mineralisation process was possibly related to
tectonically- and/or thermally-driven fluids (Figs 2.8 and 2.9, after Li et al., 1996). As
the warm to hot fluids flowed through BIFs, they deposited the iron they dissolved from
the BIF pathway in appropriate structural positions, and leached the non-iron
components (mainly SiO,) thereby concentrating the iron oxide. This model is further
elaborated by Powell et al. (1999) through basin analysis and fluid inclusion studies (see
Fig. 2.10 and further discussion in section 7).
The hypogene model differs from the supergene model in that:
• The incoming fluids for the hypogene model come from both the deeper crust
along shear zones (thrusts) formed during the orogeny, and/or from the
sedimentary (BIF) succession.

Fig. 2.7 An idealised diagram to illustrate the formation of supergene iron ore in BIF modified
from Fig. 10-13 in Morris(1987).
A. Initial reactions at X lead eventually to deep access of ground water along the fault and the
beginnings of an artesian system. Reduction of oxygen on wet magnetite surfaces in the
outcrop zone (cathode) draws electrons from ferrous to ferric reactions occurring in the
vicinity of exposed surfaces of magnetite at depth (anode), promoting growth of ore laterally
and upward in BIF. The fault could be any feature, such as a cross fold, which would allow
deep access of ground water.
B. Eventually the upward growth of the are would be stopped by the downward progression
of erosion, and further ground water movement would now progressively leach goethite
from the deposit, producing more and more friable ore.

Fig. 2.10 Synorogenic fluid model for genesis of giant Hamersley iron oxide
orebodies. Diagram shows meteoric and hot basinal fluids being expelled into
foreland basin from uplifted fold-and-thrust belt. Arrows reflect hot (dark) basinal
fluids and cooler (clear) meteoric fluids which mix and cool as they flow laterally
away from the mountain belt. At structural positions with the right physical
chemical conditions, the mixed fluids oxidise magnetite into martite, and replace
silica with recrystallised microplaty hematite (with or without extra iron dissolved
along the fluid paths) (figure modified from Powell et at, 1999).
• The fluid-flows, either along shear zones or strata, can migrate upward (Figs 2.8,
2.9 and 2.10), or migrate into the foreland basin away from the fold-and-thrust
belt (Fig. 2.10), in the hypogene model. Upward fluid movement is not expected in
the supergene enrichment process.
• The fluid circulations are driven by the combination of (a) thermal gradient
generated by either the thrusting of hotter crust over colder, but water-saturated,
crust (Figs 2.9 and 2.10) and/or by magmatic intrusions, and (b) tectonic dilation
and compression. The supergene model involves only the circulation of meteoric
fluids at a very shallow level (outgoing fluids, presumably driven by gravity only,
exit from springs in valleys or gorges - Morris, 1986).
• The ore-forming fluids are at temperature above normal geothermal gradient (25-
30·C/km), whereas the supergene model does not predict such elevated
temperature.
17

### page_32
2.4 PREVIOUS MAGNETIC STUDIES IN THE HAMERSLEY PROVINCE
The first palaeomagnetic study on the Hamersley Province iron deposits was made by
Porath and Chamalaun on the Mt Newman and Mt Tom Price mines (Porath and
Chamalaun, 1968). A remanence carried by hematite, directed mostly downward
towards the northwest with a moderate to shallow inclination, was found from both
mines. The directions from the Mt Newman mine were much better grouped than those
from the Mt Tom Price mine. On the basis of comparison with palaeomagnetic
directions of known age, Porath and Chamalaun (1968) concluded that the
mineralisation dated back to the Precambrian, not the Phanerozoic.
Clark and Schmidt (1986) reported results from another magnetic investigation in the
region. They studied both BlF and ore bodies at the Mt Tom Price and Paraburdoo
mines. In their published paper based on those results (Schmidt and Clark, 1994), they
concluded that: (1) the BIFs in the Paraburdoo and Wittenoom areas carry a pre-folding
remanence (ca. 2200 ± 100 Ma), which is directed northwesterly, shallow upwards; (2)
supergene mineralisation of martite-goethite ores, as recorded by the Paraburdoo and
Mt Tom Price ore bodies, occurred after the ca. 2000 ± 100 Ma folding event in those
regions; (3) the microplaty hematite are bodies at Tom Price and Mt Newman were
formed by burial metamorphism at about 1950 ± 100 Ma. Some of these interpretations
were challenged by Li et al. (1993).
18

### page_33
3. PALAEOPROTEROZOIC TECTONIC AND STRUCTURAL
EVOLUTION OF THE HAMERSLEY PROVINCE
3.1 SUMMARY OF TECTONIC EVOLUTION
The Hamersley Province comprises a succession of late Archaean and early Proterowic
mafic volcanic rock, shale, banded iron-formation and carbonate rock unconformably
overlying a highly deformed older Archaean granite-greenstone terrane. The base of the
succession is approximately 2800 Ma (Arndt et aI., 1991), and most of the banded iron
formations were deposited on a relatively stable platform, remote from terrestrial clastic
input, between -2600 and 2450 Ma (Morris and Horwitz, 1983; Trendall et al., 1998;
Barley et aI., 1997). The Marra Mamba Iron Formation is the oldest iron formation
(-2600 Ma, Trendall et aI., 1998), and the Dales Gorge Member of the Brockman Iron
Formation probably spans the Archaean-Proterozoic boundary (2500 Ma). The
succeeding Joffre Formation is bracketed between 2470 Ma and 2450 Ma, the age of the
overlying bimodal suite of Woongarra Rhyolite and Weeli Wolli Formation (Barley et al.,
1997).
The youngest iron formation in the Hamersley Province, the Boolgeeda Iron Formation
conformably overlies the Woongarra Formation, and is at least in part coeval with the
lower Turee Creek Group (Martin, 1999; Martin et al., 1999). The Turee Creek Group
and the unconformably overlying Lower Wyloo Group form a tectonostratigraphic
assemblage that represents a former basin, the McGrath Trough, that lay along the
southern margin of the Hamersley Province. This wedge-shaped basin, with the
thickest and coarsest clastics in the south, developed as a foreland basin in front of the
northwards-advancing Ophthalmia fold-and-thrust belt between 2450 Ma and -2200
Ma (Fig. 3.1). The Cheela Springs Basalt, which is interpreted as a continental flood
basalt, erupted near the end of the Ophthalmia orogeny (Dow et al., 1997; Martin et al.,
1997, 1998).
The Ophthalmia Fold Belt at the southern margin of the Hamersley Province is part of
the broader latitudinally-trending Proterozoic Capricorn Orogen, which separates the
Archaean Pilbara and Yilgarn cratons and preserves their amalgamation history. Tyler
and Thorne (1990) considered that the Ophthalmia Fold Belt formed by collision
between the Yilgarn and Pilbara Cratons between 2,000 and 1,600 Ma by southward
subduction of the Pilbara block and subsequent lateral escape of the rocks caught
between the converging cratons.
19

Fig. 3.1. Stratigraphic section showing units deposited in McGrath Trough and
map view of palaeocurrent vectors, each of which summarizes tens to hundreds of
individual measurements. Palaeocurrent vectors are oriented with north toward
top of page (From Powell et at, 1999).
Early geological mapping of the Hamersley Province in the 1960s identified dome-and
basin structures that were interpreted as formed by interference of two fold systems.
They have since been reinterpreted as having formed by differential strain during a
single protracted E-trending folding (Gee, 1979). Tyler and Thome (1990) recognised
that the E-trending folds appeared older in the southwestern Hamersley Province, where
they are erosionally truncated by the widespread Beasley River Quartzite, than farther
east where the Beasley River Quartzite and overlying Cheela Springs Basalt are folded
about the easterly trends. Mter the E- trending folding, a SE- to ESE-trending set of
folds was superimposed, and, as this affects the younger Ashburton Formation rocks, it
was ascribed to the late Palaeoproterozoic (-1650 to 1700 Ma) phase of convergence
between the Pilbara and Yilgam cratons.
This structural and tectonic history has been refined in the past few years by
recognising a more complete set of superimposed deformations and relating them to the
stratigraphic evolution of the basins (Table 3.1; Fig. 3.2). The oldest deformation is an
extensively-developed NE-trending set of rotational boudins and possibly rarer
intraformational recumbent folds (termed F, hereafter), best developed in the late
Archaean Marra Mamba Iron Formation in the eastern part of the Province. They could
have formed during the deposition of overlying Hamersley Group units, but the folding
is not penecontemporaneous with deposition of the strata in which they are found. The
implied NW-8E extension occurred during the latest Archaean and earliest Proterozoic

23

### page_38
(-2600 Ma to 2450 Ma).
The second deformation is the E-trending set of folds (F,), which are part of the
Ophthalmia fold-and-thrust belt. This event involved south-to-north transport of the
Hamersley Province cover above the older Archaean (>2900 Ma) granite-greenstone
basement. The folds are most intensely developed along the southern margin of the
Hamersley Province, where they form overturned to locally recumbent folds verging to
the north. In the southern margin of the Hamersley Province slivers of the granite
greenstone basement appear to have been incorporated in the fold-and-thrust belt,
where the detachment surfaces are interpreted to cut progressively deeper into the
Earth's crust. This second deformation, which in places is associated with pervasively
developed crenulation-style cleavage, was active during deposition of the Turee Creek
and lower Wyloo Groups in the McGrath Trough in front of the advancing fold-and
thrust belt. Folded unconformities, coarse terrestrial clastics derived from the south
and truncated early E-trending folds are found along the southern margin of the
McGrath Trough. A continental flood basalt, the Cheela Springs Basalt, was emplaced
in the McGrath Trough at ca. 2,200 Ma, before the final N-S shortening associated with
the Ophthalmia Orogeny (Dow et al., 1997). SE-trending mafic dykes that cut the early
F, folds could be the feeders to the flood basalt. Geological relationships combined with
SHRIMP dating of zircons show that the fold-and-thrust belt was active between -2,400
Ma and 2,200 Ma, considerably older than previously thought (Martin et al., 1998,
1999).
An interval of extension followed. The southern margin of the Pilbara Craton was rifted
and a progressive deepening of depositional environment from shallow-marine to off
shore bar and the marine turbidites records the subsidence related to the opening of the
Ashburton Trough. The deep-water turbidites of the Ashburton Formation were
deposited in a region that previously had been the uplifted source of terrestrial clastics
in the McGrath Trough. The June Hill Volcanics, in the lower part of the Ashburton
Formation, are related to this extension and have been dated at 1834 ± 2 Ma (Pidgeon
and Horwitz, 1991).
The second major shortening deformation involves SE-trending folds (F 3) and high-angle
reverse faults that deform the Ashburton Formation but pre-date the deposition of the
Mesoproterozoic Bangemall Basin cover rocks. Best estimates of the age of this
contractional deformation are between 1800 and 1650 Ma.
24

### page_39
Deformation in the western Hamersley Province after formation of these SE-trending
folds (F 3) include ENE-trending folds and steep ESE-trending faults that formed in a
dextral strike-slip regime. The age of these dextral faults and folds is not certain; they
could be the late stages of the end-Palaeoproterozoic deformation but could also be
considerably younger, possibly even Neoproterozoic.
This revised structural and stratigraphic analysis shows that the structure of the
Hamersley Province involves two major shortening events (resulting in F. and F 3), one of
which is early Palaeoproterozoic and the other end-Palaeoproterozoic. The younger
could be related to the collision of the Pilbara and Yilgarn Cratons, but the more
regional tectonic setting of the older fold belt is as yet undetermined.
3.2 Identification of F. and F in the field
3
The recognition of F. and F3 as two separate and discrete fold events is possible in the
western Hamersley Province because:
1. F. folds trend easterly and F3 folds trend southeasterly,
2. F. folds affect rocks up to, and including, the Cheela Springs Basalt, but do not
occur higher in the Wyloo Group stratigraphy, implying that F. commenced before
2,200 Ma and are no younger than the 1830 Ma June Hill Volcanics,
3. F3 folds F., in places rotating the F. folds to recumbent attitudes,
4. F3 folds occur in all rocks up to, and including, the Capricorn Formation of the Blair
Basin, thereby implying that the F 3 folds are no older than the -1,800 Ma Ashburton
Group, and no younger than the -1,650 Ma basal Bangemall Group.
5. Mapping of unconformities between the Asburton Group and the Capricorn
Formation, and between the Capricorn Formation and the Bangemall Group (Barnes,
1998; Powell, work in progress) show that there are at least two, and possibly three,
deformations in the Ashburton Formation that are lumped as the single F. folding in
the Hamersley Province. It is not yet clear whether F. in the Hamersley Province
relates to one or all of the deformations in the Ashburton/Capricorn rocks.
Refolding is especially well developed -100 km west of Paraburdoo, where the Hardey
syncline, an F. structure, is cut across by the SE-trending F. folds (see Powell and
Horwitz, 1994). In the Turner syncline, F., F., and even younger structures are
developed; excellent examples of the refolding can be seen in outcrops on the southern
slopes of Mt Nameless (Powell and Horwitz, 1994, Stop 4.2). In the Tom Price Mine, F.
is prominent in pits, especially in the southern Prongs area, where upright F. folds
deform low-angle extensional faults that post-date F• .
25

### page_40
Refolding of F. by a SE-trending set of folds also occurs in the Newman region, where
excellent examples occur in the Weeli Wolli Formation at Cathedral Gorge -20 km
northwest of Newman, in the gorges in the ranges immediately north of Newman, and
on the western side of the Nullagine road immediately north of Orebody 23. F. also
occurs in the Whaleback Mine as the large open fold controlling the shape of Orebody
29, and as smaller-scale structures in the main Mt Whale back Mine. Cross-sections
through the Whale back Mine show that the attitudes of F. axial surfaces and the low
angle Central and Eastern footwall faults are controlled by rotation around broad F.
hinges.
Despite this there is some concern about the assignment of individual structures to the
F. and F. (or younger) generations. The assignment of any particular fold to a
generation relies on consideration of a whole range of factors, some of which are
geometry and style whereas others are based on demonstration of lateral continuity and
scale. In the southwestern Hamersley Province, F. and F. can be shown to be separated
stratigraphically in their distributions, and can thus be separated in age of formation by
the Upper Wyloo Group. However, in the Newman area, the upper Wyloo Group
stratigraphy is not present, and the separation of different folds in time by mapping
their continuity into younger rocks can not be applied. The possibility remains that F.
folds in the Newman region could be considerably younger than F. in the southwestern
Hamersley Province. It is possible, though not determined, that F. in the Newman-West
Angelas region is related to the early stage of the Pilbara-Yilgarn collision coeval with
the deposition of the Ashburton Formation further west. F. in the Newman region could
thus be as young as ca. 1,830 Ma. More work is required to test this hypothesis.
The characteristics of F. and F. folds are reasonably clear as listed (Table 3.2); most of
the problems arise in areas where the overprinting relations are not widely developed,
where the axial trends are nearly co-axial, and, in the northern part of the Province,
where F. folds are open in profile and have upright to steeply southward-inclined axial
surfaces. The presence of minor parasitic folds overturned to the north, and with well
developed axial-surface cleavage, is a good indicator of F2 folds. However, in places the
F. folds are developed only at large scale, and, if the axial surfaces are upright, it is
hard to be certain whether one is dealing with F 2 or F •.
There is another issue that relates to the question of whether F. is genuinely a separate
generation of folds from the F2 folds in the eastern Hamersley Province, where in places
the younger overprinting folds are nearly, but not exactly, co-axial with F and could,

### page_42
on the basis of geometry alone, be interpreted as simply the final stages of a continuing
rotational F. deformation. This model of continuing fold formation in a rotational strain
field envisages F. as the early folds formed when the rocks were in a ductile strain
environment, with F3 being the last stages of folding as the system "locked up" by
moving into the brittle-ductile field. On the basis of geometrical relationships alone,
this model can not be disproved in the Newman-West Angelas region, and it is only
when one takes into account the stratigraphic evidence that the F. folds in the
sou thwestern Hamersley Province are are erosionally truncated by the unconformity at
the base of the Mt McGrath Formation, the beginning of the Ashburton Trough, that a
separation of the folds in time becomes possible. Most F. folds were formed before
accumulation of the Cheela Springs Basalt (-2,200 Ma) whereas the F3 folds affect rocks
as young as 1,800 Ma. Thus, in the southeastern Hamersley Province, there maybe a
hiatus of at least 400 million years between the last of F and the onset of F 3.
2
The more interesting question is whether F3 in the Newman area is the same generation
of structures as F 3 in the western Hamersley Province. This is not an easy question to
answer with certainty, as there is no unequivocal proof that there are not two NW
trending sets of folds, one developed in the east and one in the west. The interpretation
of a single set of NW -trending folds relies on consideration of lateral continuity and
Occam's razor. In relation to lateral continuity, ideally one should trace a single
structure from the western Hamersley Province into the east, and therefore conclude
that there was only one generation of structure. We have not been able to do this in the
time available, but we note that wherever putative F3 were found they overprinted F.,
and generally had the list of characteristics in Table 3.2. The other argument is the
principle of simplicity, which states that in the absence of information to the contrary it
is simpler to assume that all folds with the characteristics of F 3 belong to one, rather
than two, generations of fold.
A younger, ENE-trending generation of folds is developed in the Mt Whaleback Mine,
where it is known as F.. These F. folds are open, upright and parallel to the Mt
Whaleback Fault, a major normal fault dipping to the south-southeast. The Mt
Whaleback Fault (and other equivalent faults such as the Homestead Fault) is
considered by Tyler et aL (1990) to be related to the formation of the Blair Basin, a
molassic-style basin developed late during the Ashburton Orogeny, but before
deposition of the overlying Bangemall Basin. F. may have formed at the same time as
the Mt Whale back normal fault, or afterwards during a phase of mild compression. NE
trending folds elsewhere in the eastern Hamersley Province cut across F3 structures,
28

### page_43
and thus F. is considered by us to be a late Ashburton generation of folds, possibly
between 1700 and 1650 Ma.
The youngest generation of structures in the eastern Hamersley Province are N- to
NNW-trending broad warps, which we call here F• . F. occurs in the Mt Whaleback area,
where it can be seen in "Death Valley" north of the open cut (Ascott and Powell, 1995).
F affects the main structure in the Mt Whaleback open pit, where it causes a reversal
5
of the generally WSW-plunging F. structures in the western half of the pit. The age of F.
is not known, other than it is younger than F.. It could be related to late
Mesoproteroroic or Neoproterozoic deformation.
29

### page_44
4. SAMPLING AND TECHNIQUES
4.1 SAMPLING AND SPECIMEN PREPARATION
Four field trips were carried out during this project: one in late May to early June 1995,
one in November 1995, one in late May to early June 1996, and the last one in late
June to early July 1997. Five hundred and seventy-eight (578) oriented samples were
collected from one hundred and fifteen (liS) sites. About 70% of the samples were
collected as oriented blocks, mostly because of the unusual hardness of the rocks which
makes on-site drilling with a portable drill difficult. The samples are located in six
subregions shown in Figure 1.1: i.e., the Newman region (Fig. 4.1), the West Angelas
and Area C region (Fig. 4.2), the Tom Price (Turner Syncline) region (Fig. 4.3), the
Paraburdoo region (Fig. 4.4), the Duck Creek region (Fig. 4.5), and the Hamersley
Chichester Ranges region (Fig. 4.6). At rock formation level, the distribution of these
samples is: 5 (1 site) in the Boongal Formation,S (1) in the Pyradie Formation, 45 (7) in
the Bunjinah Formation, 13 (2) in the Jeerinah Formation, 55 (12) in the Marra Mamba
Iron Formation, 76 (13) in the Wittenoom Formation, 28 (8) in the Mount Sylvia
Formation,9 (1) in the Mount McRae Shale, 205 (46) in the Brockman Iron Formation,
27 (6) in the Weeli Wolli Formation, 18 (3) in the Woongarra Rhyolite, 38 (6) in the
Boolgeeda Iron Formation, 17 (2) in the Turee Creek Dolomite, 9 (2) in the Cheela
Springs Basalt, 6 (1) in the Mount McGrath Formation, 10 (2) in the Duck Creek
Dolomite, and 6 (2) in dolerite dykes. All sampling sites are listed in Table 4.1.
One hundred and nine samples were from iron ores: 69 (17 sites) from martite
microplaty hematite ores, and 40 (9 sites) from the martite-goethite and martite
((goethite)) ores. A magnetic compass and a sun compass were used to orient the
samples. Bedding measurements were taken wherever possible. Block samples were re
drilled into 25 mm-diameter core samples using a table drill in the UWA laboratory.
Each 25 mm-diameter core sample was cut into one to four (mostly two or three)
standard 22-mm height palaeomagnetic specimens.
For the purpose of testing the ages of the remanent magnetisation recorded in rocks,
both fold test and conglomerate test were designed when possible during sampling.
Most sampling sites were from road-cuts, river beds or open pits, so as to minimise the
effects of lightning and weathering. Locations of each sampling site are shown in
Figures 4.1-4.6.
30

4.2 MAGNETIC SUSCEPTIBILITY AND ANISOTROPY MEASUREMENTS
Magnetic petrophysics analysis is necessary for better understanding of the magnetic
remanence results, and more importantly, for correct interpretation of aero-magnetic
anomalies. Petrophysical analysis was carried out by W. Guo as part of his PhD
research. We present here all the major findings. More detailed discussions can be
found in W. GUo's PhD thesis to be submitted during 1999 (Guo, 1999).
Magnetic foliation pole Given an anisotropy ellipsoid of

The magnetic foliation plane contains the maximum and intermediate susceptibility
axes. The magnetic lineation is parallel to the maximum susceptibility axis.
Anisotropy of low-field magnetic susceptibility was measured in the Palaeomagnetic
Laboratory of UW A using a Bartington MS2 susceptibility/anisotropy system. Volume
susceptibility and a six-position measuring procedure were adopted in all the AMS
measurements. A total of one thousand, one hundred and forty-six AMS data sets were
obtained. All measurements were made within a one-layer magnetic shield.
43

### page_58
4.3 MAGNETIC REMANENCE AND DEMAGNETISATION TECHNIQUES
Palaeomagnetism studies the Earth's history (either regional or global) through
analysing the magnetic vectors (magnetic remanence, or remanent magnetisation)
recorded in rock formations or bodies since their formation. A magnetic remanence is a
vector. Its direction can be expressed by its declination (D), which is the angular
difference between the dip-direction of the remanence and the geographic north, and its
inclination (I), the angle between the remanence vector and the horizontal plane (Fig.
4.8). The inclination angle in a given rock body (assuming only one remanence is
involved, and the remanence was restored to the palaeohorizontal at which it was
acquired) is related to the palaeolatitude (A) at which the remanence was acquired by
function:
tan (I) = 2 tan (A),
and its declination angle reflects the deviation of the relevant continent (or a fragment of
it) from its original orientation when the remanence was acquired.
North
Fig. 4.8 An illustration of
magnetic declination (D) and
inclination (I). A upward
directed remanence vector
will have a negative
Magnetic inclination.
remanence
Down vector
There are different ways for a rock unit to acquire a magnetic remanence. Sedimentary
rocks can acquire a remanence either during the depositional process (when small
suspended magnetic particles are aligned by the Earth's geomagnetic field), which is
called the depositional remanent magnetisation (DRMJ, or during the post-depositional
process which includes: (1) the diagenesis, (2) mineral recrystaIlisation due to a
(thermo)-chemical event (chemical remanent magnetisation, or CRMJ) , (3) a thermal
remanent magnetisation (TRMJ purely due to a thermal event, and (4) a viscous remanent
magnetisation (VRMJ acquired through a long-time exposure to a magnetic field at room
temperature. A magmatic rock can acquire a thermal remanence when it is cooled
below the Curie temperatures of magnetic minerals (e.g. -675°C for hematite, and
-575°C for magnetite), but, like sedimentary rocks, it can also be remagnetised by
44

### page_59
younger events. Lightning strikes can also reset part or all of the magnetic remanence
in a rock outcrop.
Magnetic remanence recorded during the formation of rocks is called primary remanent
magnetisation, and remanence acquired since then, either due to changes in thermal
and! or chemical conditions, or due to viscous origin, is called secondary remanent
magnetisation. The combination of primary (if it still exists) and secondary remanent
magnetisation in a particular rock body forms its natural remanent magnetisation (NRM)
(Fig. 4.9).
Fig. 4.9 An example of a NRM
consisting of two remanence
vectors (vectors I & 2). Dashed
vectors are the remanent vectors
measured after each step of
demagnetisation.
Down Remanence vector
..... ..0 measured during stepwise
demagnetisation
In order to delineate the individual remanence vectors (both their direction and
intensity) from the total NRM, stepwise demagnetisation is normally performed in the
laboratory, and the remanent magnetisation in the samples is measured after each step
of demagnetisation. The most commonly-used demagnetisation methods are thermal
demagnetisation, where specimens are heated and cooled in a magnetic-free space in
successive demagnetisation steps, and alternating field (AF) demagnetisation, where a
specimen is subjected to the "hammering" of an alternating field in a shielded
environment with the field intensity decaying from a set value to zero. In ideal
situations, the different phases of remanent magnetisation are shown in
demagnetisation curves as vectors with different demagnetisation spectra (e.g., vectors 1
and 2 in Figure 4.9).
It should be noted that the magnetic behaviour of hematite, magnetite and goethite are
quite distinctive (see more discussion in section 5.4 and a summary in Table 5.18).
However, the magnetic behaviour of martite, a form of hematite, can not be easily
distinguished from that of microplaty hematite (both have a Curie temperature of
-680°C). In Chapter 6 on magnetic remanence we use hematite to refer to both mineral
phases.
45

### page_60
A number of field tests can be used to determine the age of a remanent magnetisation,
e.g., conglomerate test, fold test, backed contact test, etc. The question these tests are
used to address is whether the magnetisation was acquired before or after the erosion of
the conglomerate (conglomerate test). the folding (fold test). or the intrusion of the dyke
or sill (backed contact test). This is done through comparing the pattern of
magnetisation expected in each case with the measured distribution.
The fold test is a particularly important test in this study. The way it works is that
magnetisation acquired before folding will be rotated with the bedding (Fig. 4. lOa), and
thus will be more scattered than it would be if the fold limbs were restored to a common
(horizontal) orientation. On the other hand, magnetisation acquired after folding will be
better-grouped in-situ (Fig. 4.1Ob) than after the strata were restored to horizontal. We
can thus assess the relative age of the magnetisation by comparing the degree of
dispersion before and after unfolding.
a. Remanence Acquired before Folding
b. Remanence Acquired ailer Folding
Fig. 4.10 Cartoons illustrating the fold test.
From the geographic locations of a rock unit and its remanence direction (presumably
at the correct palaeo horizontal in which the remanence was acquired). one can then
calculate the position of a corresponding palaeopole. By connecting palaeo poles for a
given rigid crustal block according to their age sequence, one can establish the
46

### page_61
palaeomagnetic fingerprint of that continent, which is called the apparent polar wander
path (APWP). For more information about the fundamentals of palaeomagnetism we
refer readers to Chapters 2 and 4 of a book by Van der Voo (1993).
In this study, a 2G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer was used for the measurement
of remanent magnetisation. Two MMTD2 IS-sample thermal demagnetisers and a 2G
automated AF demagnetiser attached to the cryogenic magnetometer were used for
demagnetisation process. A MMPM9 pulse magnetiser was employed for magnetising
specimens during isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM) experiments. The natural
remanent magnetisation (NRM) of 1014 specimens was measured. Demagnetisation,
normally with 12-16 steps, but up to 20 steps for some specimens, was carried out for
at least one specimen from each sample. Whenever necessary, extra specimens were
demagnetised. In total 611 specimens were treated by either thermal or AF
demagnetisation. Thirteen specimens were selected for IRM experiments.
In addition to magnetic measurements, XRD and XRF analyses of forty-three samples
were conducted in the X-Ray Analytical Laboratory of the Department of Geology and
Geophysics at UWA. These results are discussed and incorporated into the magnetic
data interpretation.
47

### page_62
5 MAGNETIC PETROPHYSICS
5.1 MEAN BULK SUSCEPTIBILITY (MBS) RESULTS
5.1.1 MBS of BIFs
All five main iron formations of the Hamersley Group show a similar distribution
pattern of mean bulk susceptibility (MBS) - a logarithmic bimodal distribution (Fig. 5.1),
particularly in the Brockman, Wee Ii Wolli and Boolgeeda BIFs. This means that each
iron formation has two major susceptibility groups. The difference between the centres
of the two groups for each iron formation is usually greater than one order of
magnitude.
Marra Mamba Iron Formation
The Marra Mamba Iron Formation, the oldest iron formation in the Hamersley Group,
generally shows a low magnetic susceptibility. The 'higher susceptibility population has
an arithmetic (i.e. average) MBS of 142 ± 87 x 10.5 SI (Table 5.1), and occurs in 50% of
the total specimens. Hematite is the dominant magnetic mineral in these specimens.
The lower susceptibility population has a MBS of only 36 ± 16 x 10.5 SI. These samples
are either chert- or goethite-dominated. The population percentage-based average of
MBS, which is only used as an indicator for comparison with other rocks in the basin, is
89 x 10.5 SI. The highest bulk susceptibility recorded in the Marra Mamba Iron
Formation is 420 x 10.5 SI, which is carried by a BIF sample near a northwesterly
trending dolerite dyke northwest of Newman.

All site MBS values are listed in Table 5.2. Site MM01 from the southern limb of the
Turner Syncline has the highest site-mean of lSI ± 97 x 10-5 , whereas site MM05 from
the northern limb of the Turner Syncline has the lowest site-mean of 21 ± 18 x H)"5 SI
in both the Marra Mamba Iron Formation and the entire Hamersley Group BIFs.
Mount Sylvia Fonnation
The BIF samples of the Mt Sylvia Formation were collected mostly from Brunos Band
and commonly show high susceptibility. The higher population gives a MBS of 4523 ±
2724 x 10.5 SI (Table 5.1) and the corresponding samples contain a detectable fraction
of magnetite (see MF02B and MF03C in Table 5.11). Specimens within the higher MBS
group account for 65.4% of all the specimens. The lower popUlation has a BMS of only
430 ± 299 x 10.5 SI, but it is still much higher than the high MBS value of the Marra
Mamba Iron Formation. Samples in the lower population have relatively less magnetite
compared with the higher popUlation. The population percentage-based average of
MBS is 3107 x 10-5 SI.
The highest bulk susceptibility recorded in the Mount Sylvia Formation is 10252 x 10.5
SI, which is carried by a BIF sample nearly on the top of Mount Governor in the West
Angelas area. On the basis of site means, all sites show a MBS higher than 1000 x 10-5
SI, except site MF06 around Mount Bruce which has a MBS of 843 x 10-5 SI (Table 5.2).
Site MF07 from Mount Governor of the West Angelas area has the highest site MBS of
4654 ± 4317 x 10.5 SI.
Brockman Iron Fonnation
The Brockman Iron Formation, the major host formation for the martite-microplaty
hematite ore in the Hamersley Iron Province, also shows high susceptibility. The higher
population has a MBS of 4258 ± 2887 x 10.5 SI (Table 5.1), which accounts for 51.8% of
the total specimens. The lower population has a MBS of only 329 ± 240 x 10-5 SI.
Samples in the low MBS population are weathered and chert-rich BIFs. The popUlation
percentage-based average of MBS is 2364 x 10-5 SI. The highest bulk susceptibility
recorded in the Brockman Iron Formation is 12282 x 10.5 SI.
For the Brockman Iron Formation, however, on the member level, the MBS of the Joffre
Member BIFs exhibits a logarithmic normal distribution, whereas that of the Dales
Gorge Member BIFs still shows a weak bimodal distribution (Fig. 5.2). The MBS of the

On the basis of site means, the highest MBS is 10354 ± 1479 x 10-5 SI from site BM04

in site OB25-3 of Orebody 25 have the lowest site MBS of 106 ± 17 x 10-5 SI.
Weeli WoW Formation
The higher population of the We eli Wolli Formation BIFs has a MBS of 5361 ± 2849 x
10.5 SI (Table 5.1), which corresponds with samples containing more
magnetite/maghemite. Specimens within the higher population account for 59% of the
total specimens. The lower population has a MBS of 352 ± 214 x 10-5 SI. The
population percentage-based average of MBS is 3307 x 10.5 SI. The highest bulk
susceptibility recorded in the Weeli Wolli Formation is 17000 x 10-5 SI from a BIF
sample in the northern limb of the Turner Syncline.
On the basis of site means, all other sites have MBS higher than 1000 x 10-5 SI, except
for site WW05 from northwest of Newman which has a MBS of 222xlO'5 SI (Table 5.2).
Site WWO 1 in the northern limbs of the Turner Syncline has the highest site MBS of
·5708 X 10-5 SI. Both site WW02 from the southern limb of the Turner Syncline and site
WW06 from the Duck Creek area have site MBS in the range of 5200-5500 x 10-5 SI.
Boolgeeda Iron Formation
Samples of different lithology were collected from the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. Sites
BIO 1-03 and BI05 consist mainly of mudstone with minor BIFs, whereas the samples of
the site BI06 are weathered M-(mpl h) ore. Only samples from site BI04 are typical BIF.
The bulk susceptibilities of the Boolgeeda Iron Formation samples show a weak
logarithmic bimodal distribution (Fig. 5.1a) with a small portion of the high
susceptibility population (17%) having a MBS of 6018 ± 4536 x 10-5 SI. The lower
susceptibility population has a MBS of 87 ± 48 x 10-5 SI. The population percentage
based average of MBS is 1095 x 10.5 SI. The highest bulk susceptibility recorded in the
Boolgeeda Iron Formation is 14000 x 10.5 SI from a BIF sample in the southern limb of
the Turner Syncline.
On the basis of site means, all other sites have MBS below 150 x 10-5 SI, with site BI04
from the southern limb of the Turner Syncline being the only exception (MBS = 6018 x

10.5 SI) (Table 5.2). Site BI03 in the Duck Creek area has the lowest site MBS of 37 x
10.5 SI.
Regional variations in MBS of the Hamersley Group BIFs
In order to see if there is any regional variation in the MBS, we subdivided the
Hamersley Iron Province into four major regions: the Newman and West Angelas-Area C
region as the east region, the Duck Creek sampling areas as the west region, the Tom
Price and Paraburdoo sampling areas as the central region, and the Hamersley Range
and Chichester Ranges region as the north region. The compiled data are listed in
Table 5.3. Because only half of the groupings (highlighted in bold) satisfY the minimum
sample number (thirty) required for a meaningful statistics (Johnson and
Bhattacharyya, 1996), any regional comparison should be treated with caution. A
major noticeable feature is that the MBS for Brockman BlFs in the northern region is
significantly higher than that for the other regions.

5.1.2 MBS of iron ores
On the formation level, both the Brockman and Marra Mamba iron ores exhibit a
logarithmic normal distribution and have very similar bulk susceptibility values (Fig.
5.3). The only noticeable difference between them is that the Brockman ores have
higher percentage of high bulk susceptibility, possibly resulting from the dolerite
intrusions within ore bodies. As a result, the Brockman ores show a slightly higher
arithmetic MBS (K = 343 ± 197 x 10.5 SI, with a coefficient of variation Cv = 0.5743) than
the Marra Mamba ores (K = 285 ± 117 x 10.5 SI, Cv = 004105) (Table 504). Compared
with both the Brockman and Marra Mamba ores, the MBS of the Barrett-

MBS of Brockman iron deposits
The susceptibility distribution of major Brockman ore bodies studied are shown in
Figure 5.4 and listed in Table 5.5. The Mount Whaleback mine, Orebody 25, the Tom
Price mine and the combined Channar-Paraburdoo deposits all show a logarithmic
normal distribution (Fig. 5.4). However, the bulk susceptibility of the Whale back ores is
the best grouped (Table 5.5d). The magnetic susceptibility of the Tom Price ores (K =
419 ± 217 x 10-5 SI, Cv = 0.5179) is very similar to that of the Orebody 25 in both their
MBS and coefficient of variation, although dolerite intrusion in the Tom Price mine is
extensive whereas no dyke has been found in Orebody 25. The M-(mpl h) ore samples
from the Paraburdoo mine give a relevatively low, but well-grouped (Cv = 0.398) mean
MBS of 196 x 10-5 SI. M-(mpl h) ore samples from the Channar and Paraburdoo
deposits give a combined MBS of 268 ± 204 x 10.5 SI with Cv = 0.7612).
If the Whale back mine and Orebody 25 are combined as the eastern mining area, and
the Channar, Paraburdoo and Tom Price mines together as the western mining area, the
bulk susceptibilities of the two mining areas still follow the logarithmic normal
distribution (Fig. 5.5) and share a similar MBS around 340 x 10-5 SI after the dolerite
affected samples in the western mining area are excluded (Table 5.5). The difference
between them is obvious, i.e., the western area has a wider range of susceptibility than
the eastern area. This difference is also reflected by a smaller Cv for the eastern area
(0.6383 and 0.5029 before, and after, removing some high susceptibility readings,

respectively), and a higher Cv for the western area (1.9646 and 0.6607 before, and after,
removing some high susceptibility readings respectively).

5.1.3 MBS of other Fortescue and Hamersley Groups rocks
The MBS of all other rock units studied, together with that of the BIF units and ore
bodies, are summarised in Table 5.7, and plotted in Figure 5.6. The MBS of the non
BIF and non-ore rock units are all below 100 x 10.5 SI, and therefore would play little
role in magnetic modelling.
5.2 ANISOTROPY OF MAGNETIC SUSCEPTIBILITY (AMS) RESULTS
The average degree of magnetic anisotropy for each individual site is given in Table 5.2.
The orientation of the magnetic fabric, as well as the variation of the anisotropy degree
between rock formations (Table 5.8) and geographic locations (Table 5.9), is briefly
discussed below.
5.2.1 AMS ofBIFs
There are three major types of AMS results from the six BIF units in the Hamersley Iron
Province: (1) Well-developed, bedding-parallel or bedding sub-parallel magnetic foliation,
as represented by the Brunos Band (e.g. MF07), Dales Gorge BIF (e.g. BM02), Joffre BlF
(e.g. BM07), and Wee Ii Wolli BIF (e.g. WW06) (Fig. 5.7). The average degree of
anisotropy for these BIFs is normally ,,1.1 and can be up to 4.7 (Table 5.8). (2)
Recognisable sub-bedding-parallel magnetic foliation, as exemplified by the Boolgeeda
BIFs (Fig. 5.8). The average degree of anisotropy for this type is around, or less than,
1.1, and the maximum degree of anisotropy of any individual specimen is below 1.5. (3)
Very weak or no magnetic foliation that is commonly oblique to the bedding plane. This
type is found in the Marra Mamba BIFs only (Fig. 5.9).
In term of the magnitude of anisotropy, there is a non-normal distribution for all the
BIF units (Fig. 5.10). Most of the samples have an AMS degree between 1.0 and 1.2:
>90% for the Marra Mamba and Boolgeeda BIFs, >70% for the Weeli Wolli, Joffre and
Dales Gorge (thus Brockman) BIFs, and about 45% for the Brunos Band samples. No
AMS values over 1.8 have been found from the Marra Mamba and Boolgeeda BIFs, but
they account for -10% of the samples in the Weeli Wolli, Joffre and Dales Gorge BlFs,
and 15% in Brunos Band. The average value for each BIF unit, and their maximum
ranges, are shown in Figure 5.11.

As the MBS of the Mount Sylvia (Brunos Band), Dales Gorge, Joffre and Weeli Wolli
BIFs are all over 0.01 or 1000 x 10.5 SI, the effects of AMS on magnetic modelling
should not be ignored. The degree of anisotropy of the Boolgeeda and Marra Mamba
BIFs can be regarded as very low (A < 1.1), and their influence on magnetic modelling is
thus negligible.
Marra Mamba Iron Fonnation
Generally, BIFs of the Marra Mamba Iron Formation show very low AMS without
remarkable bedding-parallel magnetic foliation. All the six sampling sites exhibit
average degrees of anisotropy between· 1.055-1.085 (Table 5.2). As a result, no evident
difference in AMS can be seen between different regions (Table 5.9).
69

### page_84
Mount Syillia Formation (Brunos Band)
In contrast with the Marra Mamba BIFs, Brunos Band BlFs have weJI-developed
bedding-parallel or sub-parallel magnetic foliation (Fig. 5.7b). The six sampling sites
have an average degree of anisotropy of 1.476, which is the highest unit-mean value in
the Hamersley Group BlF units (Table 5.8, Fig. 5.10).

RegionaJIy, Brunos Band in the eastern region has the highest average degree of

of anisotropy of 1.283 and 1.114, respectively. It should be noticed that there was only
one sampling site from quite weathered BIFs in the northern region. The relatively
lower degree of anisotropy in this region may not reflect the true properties of fresh
BIFs. The highest four anisotropy readings (6.160, 3.662, 2.966 and 2.818) recorded in
this BIF unit were all from the West Angelas-Area C sampling area (sites MF07 and
AC04).
Brockman Iron Formation
Dales Gorge Member
Similar to the Brunos Band BIFs, the Dales Gorge Member BIFs have weJI-developed
bedding-parallel or sUb-paraJIel magnetic foliation (Fig. 5.7d). The sixteen sampling
sites show an average degree of anisotropy of 1.298, which is the second highest unit
mean value in the Hamersley Group BIF units.
RegionaJIy, within the Dales Gorge Member, the average degree of anisotropy tends to
decrease from northern (1.702), eastern (1.210), to the central and western (-1.16)
regions. The northern region also has the highest regional mean value in aJI the
70

### page_85
Hamersley Group BIF units (Table 5.9). It should be noticed that because there was
only one sampling site from both the central and the western regions, the relatively
lower anisotropy there may not reflect the true property of fresh BIFs. Site BM06 in
Vampire Gorge of the northern region has the highest site-mean degree of anisotropy
(2.762) recorded in the Dales Gorge Member BIFs (Table 5.2) as well as in all the BIF
sampling sites in the Hamersley Group. Three of the five individual anisotropy readings
higher than 3.0 occurred in this site. However, the highest anisotropy reading (4.749)
in this member came from site DG03 in the Cathedral Gorge near Newman.
Joffre Member
The Joffre Member BIFs show very similar AMS features to the Dales Gorge Member
BIFs, i.e., well-developed bedding-parallel or sub-parallel magnetic foliation with an
average degree of anisotropy of 1.202 but a smaller variation (Fig. 5.7c, Table 5.8). Site
TP09 at the Tom Price mine in the central region has the highest site-mean degree of
anisotropy of 1.632 (Table 5.2).
Weeli Wolli Fonnation
The Weeli Wolli BIFs also have well-developed bedding-parallel or sub-parallel magnetic
foliation (Fig. 5.7a). The six sampling sites show an average degree of anisotropy of
1.240, and individual specimens have values up to 3.681 (Table 5:8). Site WWOl from
the northern limb of the Turner Syncline has the highest site-mean anisotropy of 1.878
for this formation (Table 5.2).
Regionally, the eastern and northern regions have low average degree of anisotropy of
1.058 and 1.140, respectively. The central and western regions have average degree of
anisotropy of 1.474 and 1.219, respectively. There was only one sampling site each for
the western and eastern regions, and two sampling sites each for the northern and
central regions. Such a low regional sampling density suggests that the results may not
be representative.
Boolgeeda Iron Fonnation
Although there are recognisable bedding-parallel or SUb-parallel magnetic foliation in
the Boolgeeda BIFs (Fig. 5.8), all six sampling sites have low average degree of
anisotropy of less than 1.2 (Tables 5.2 and 5.8). No evident regional variation in AMS
has been detected (Table 5.9).

5.2.2 AMS of iron ores and other geological units
AMS ofI ron Ores
All the iron deposits are characterised by weak AMS and the average degree of
anisotropy of individual deposits is within 1.042-1.070 (Table 5.10). In the other words,
all iron ores are close to isotropic in susceptibility. In a few cases, a weak sub-bedding
parallel magnetic foliation can be recognised (Fig. 5.12).
AMS of Other Geological Units
Other rock units are generally isotropic. Dolomite, shales and Woongarra Rhyolite, are
featured with low MBS «100 x 10.5 SI), but slightly higher than average degree of
anisotropy (Table 5.9). No regional pattern of magnetic fabric can be seen for those rock
units.
The Cheela Springs Basalt and a dolerite dyke showed localised high bulk susceptibility
with very low AMS.
Detailed discussions on estimation of MBS and AMS for magnetic modelling can be
found in Guo (1999).
73

### page_88
5.3 NRM directions and intensities
Both the direction and intensity of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) of a rock
unit, and its relationship with the bedding attitude in the case of bedded rocks, are
important for correct interpretation of magnetic anomaly data. The matter is relatively
simple when there is only one phase of dominant remanent magnetisation in the rock
unit. However, the situation can be complicated when several phases of remanent
magnetisation are involved, and the NRM represents a vector-sum of all the remanence.
We document here the overall characteristics of the NRM directions and intensities only.
For composition of the NRM in various rock units and localities one is referred to
section 6: Palaeomagnetism Results. For more detailed analysis of NRM information
and applications to magnetic modelling, one is inferred to the PhD thesis of W. Guo
(1999).
5.3.1 NRM ofBIFs and iron ores
The arithmetic mean [Mean = (Ml + M2 + M3 + ... + Mn)/nl and Geometric mean (a
geometric mean of n numbers is the nth root of their product) of NRM intensities of the
rock formations are given in Table 5.11. The vector-mean directions and intensities of
both the rock formations and iron ores are listed in Table 5.12. As shown in Figure
5.13, the NRM directions of the BIF samples are quite scattered in geographic
coordinates, although concentrations of directions can be seen in all formations. In
contrast with the BlFs, NRM directions in the iron ore deposits normally show a good
degree of agreement: dominantly westerly-downward directions in the Whale back
deposit and Orebody 25 (Fig. 5.14a), and northwesterly directions in the other deposits
(Fig.5.14b-c). All deposits, except the West Angelas and Area C deposits, where some
samples may have been subjected to lightning strikes, give an average remanence
intensity of the same order of magnitude.
5.3.2 NRM of other rock units
As shown in Table 5.13, the NRM intensity of these non-B1F samples are generally one
to two orders of magnitude lower than BIFs; their significance for magnetic modelling is
minimal.
74

5.3.3 Q Values of BIFs, iron ores and other rock units in the Hamersley Basin
Q Values of surface BIF samples
Q value is the ratio between the remanent and induced magnetisation of a rock
formation. The site-mean Q values of BIF units are given in Table 5.14. A few severely
weathered sites were excluded from the list.
In general, the sampling sites located in deep creek-cuts, caves or open-pits, where the
chances of being lightning-struck are rare, normally have average Q values < 2. On the
other hand, sampling sites on tops of hills or ridges, where lightning strikes are more
common events, normally have average Q values> 10. There are also sampling sites
(e.g., sites MM05 and BMO I) in open creek beds, where lightning strikes are also
possible, with average Q values between 5 and 15.
Q Values of iron ores
The deposit-mean Q values are given in Table 5.15. The ore samples from the Mount
Whale back, Tom Price, Paraburdoo and Channar deposits are sampled in open pits, and
they are unlikely to have been affected by lightning. Samples from the Barrett-Lennard
deposit are from a natural exposure at a topographic low, and thus lightning is also an
unlikely event there. The average Q values of these deposits range between 5 and 18.
However, samples of Marra Mamba martite-goethite ores are mostly from natural 'hard
caps' exposures, and their extraordinary high mean Q values (Table 5.15) probably
reflect lightning strikes.

All the mean Q values of non-BIF sites are listed in Table 5.16. Within the five sites

5.4 Magnetic mineralogy of BIFs and iron ores, and their relevance to
susceptibility
Magnetic mineralogy analysis was undertaken to understand the magnetic carriers for
various remanence components, as well as the variations in other magnetic
x
petrophysical properties. XRD analysis of 43 selected samples was carried out in the
Ray Analytical Laboratory of the Department of Geology and Geophysics at UWA (Table
5.11). Compared with other techniques such as the acquisition and demagnetisation of
isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM), demagnetisation of natural remanent
magnetisation, and thermal variation of low-field magnetic susceptibility (K-TJ, this is
the only direct and quantitative analytical technique. However, the drawback of this
technique is that it is insensitive to magnetic minerals less than I % of the total mass,
and to ultrafine-grained rock.
As shown in Table 5.17, three major magnetic phases, magnetite, hematite(martite) and
goethite, have been identified from the analysed samples. Hematite has been found in
all samples, with its weight percentage various between 14.4% and 99.8%. Twenty-five
samples (58%) have magnetite weighted between 1.1% and 12.4%. Thirty-one samples
(72%) contain goethite weighted between 1.8% and 32.3%. It is interesting to note that
any magnetite in the surface samples from the Boolgeeda and Marra Mamba BlFs, as
well as in the ore samples, is below the detectable level (1 %). It is also noticeable that
the presence of sulphur, likely in sulfide minerals such as pyrite and pyrrhotite) in
many samples, including some of the ore samples. This could explain the generation of
secondary magnetite during many of the susceptibility/temperature (K-T) experiments
(see discussion below). In only three of the seven M-(mpl h) ore samples, goethite has
been detected. Note that in both XRD and magnetic analysis martite is
indistinguishable from microplaty hematite.
Results of various magnetic analysis confirm the XRD results, but in some cases they
revealed trace amount of magnetic minerals which are otherwise undetectable with XRD
analysis. The most systematic magnetic information of all is the demagnetisation of

natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), which has been applied to every sample
collected. This technique utilises the different Curie/Neel temperatures for different
magnetic minerals (Table 5.18), above which the minerals lose their magnetisation, to
distinguish these minerals. The general trend is that both hematite and magnetite can
dominate the magnetism in BIF samples, but goethite occurs only sporadically as the
main magnetic mineral in Marra Mamba BIFs. In ore samples, hematite is almost
always the dominant magnetic carrier, and the sometime occurrence of a trace amount
of magnetite is commonly related to contact with dykes. Magnetic mineralogy
interpretations for each site based on this technique can be found in section 6:
Palaeomagnetism Results.
Isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM) and thermal variation of low-field magnetic
susceptibility (K-T) experiments have been conducted on selected samples. The IRM
84

### page_99
method distinguishes magnetic minerals using their magnetic coercivities (magnetite
easily gets saturated by an applied field, whereas hematite, pyrrhotite and goethite are
much harder to get saturated), and K-T analysis again utilises the different Curie/Nee!
temperatures for different magnetic minerals (Table 5.18). The K-T measurements were
conducted using the Bartington system driven by the GEOLAB software package. The
maximum temperature reached was 710· C. The measurements were made within a
'one-Iayer magnetic shield. A few typical results of these analysis are shown in Figures
5.15 and 5.16.
The relationships between the magnetite/hematite contents and mean magnetic
susceptibility in the samples analysed are shown in Figure 5.17. It is interesting to note
that there is no correlation between the bulk susceptibility and hematite content in
samples that have magnetite content> I wt% (Fig. S.17a). In those samples, a power
law exists between the bulk susceptibility and magnetite content (Fig. 5.17b). However,
in samples with magnetite content < I wt%, an exponential law can be established
between bulk susceptibility and hematite content (Fig. S.17c). More detailed
discussions of those analyses and their implications for magnetic modeling can be
found in Guo (1999).
