### page_104
6 PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
SUMMARY
Five phases of remanent magnetisation have been identified from the Hamersley
Province:
(I) A possible primary remanence from four sampling sites in the little-deformed
Fortescue Group volcaniclastic rocks. The A.s of the average pole position
reduces from 64.3· in-situ to 32.7· after bedding correction of two of the sites,
whereas the other two sites are flat-lying, indicating a possible pre-tilting origin.
But there are uncertainties as to which generation of folding tilted the bedding.
The remanence occurs as the high-temperature component carried by magnetite.
(2) A post-F., pre-F., and possibly pre-F., magnetic overprint that is pervasive in
the Newman, West Angelas and Area C regions, becoming less prominent in the
Tom Price and Paraburdoo regions, and totally laCking in the western (Duck Creek
region) and northern (Hamersley and Chichester Ranges) Hamersley Province. It
is the most stable magnetic component where it coexists with other components,
and is commonly carried by hematite/martite, but in places also by magnetite.
The overprint is believed to be of thermal/ chemical (mostly chemical) origin. The
age of the remanence is probably toward the end of the Ophthalmia Orogeny, e.g.,
ca. 2200 Ma, but vould be as young as ca. 1700 Ma.
(3) A late to post-F. magnetic overprint that is widespread in the western, central
and northern Hamersley Province, but less prominent in the eastern Hamersley
Province. It can be carried by either magnetite and hematite/martite, and in
some places possibly by maghemite. Where it coexists with the above-mentioned
two components, it occurs as the lower-temperature component. It appears to be
of mostly chemical origin in iron ores and BIFs, of thermal/ chemical origin in
carbonate (in which this overprint is pervasive), and mostly thermal origin in not
so-porous volcanic rocks. The temperature of the thermal overprint in some of
the volcanic rocks is estimated to have been ca. 250 ± 100·C according to
Middleton and Schmidt's (1982) theoretical T-t chart. It is believed to be related
to the late stage of F. deformation, i.e. the Ashburton Orogeny, with an age of ca.
1700 Ma, but could be younger.
(4) A preliminary remanent direction from five samples of baked rocks in, and
around, a NE-trending dolerite dyke in Channar Mine, which fall close to the pole
position of the 755 ± 3 Ma Mundine Well dyke swarm in western Pilbara (Wingate
and Giddings, 1999). This suggests that the NE-trending dyke probably belongs to
the Mundine Well dyke swarm.
90

### page_105
(5) Late Cretaceous (?) to Cenozoic overprints reflecting either weathering or
viscous remanent magnetisation. This remanence is best developed in dolomite,
volcanic rocks and BIFs, but rarely seen clearly In the studied ore bodies.
Whereas overprints of weathering origin are normally carried by hematite, and
rarely by maghemite and goethite, viscous overprints are normally carried by
magnetite.
6.1 MT WHALEBACK MINE, SATELLITE ORE BODIES 23 AND 25, AND ADJACENT
REGIONS (Table 6.1; Fig. 4.1)
Summary
The majority of samples, either from the martite-microplaty hematite ore bodies
(i.e. the Mt Whaleback Mine), martlte-goethite ores (Orebodies 23 and 25), or BIFs,
=
revealed a post-F. . pre-F. remanence with a mean direction (NM1) of D 248.7·, I
= 62.9· (N = 13, a.s = 11.S· and K = 13.4). The remanence is carried by a variety of
magnetic minerals which suggest a major chemical/thermal event in the region
that was responsible for the oxidation of magnetite into martite and the
crystallisation of microplaty hematite, therefore likely the formation of these ore
bodies. Remanence from the contact zone of a NW-trending dyke agrees with this
presumed ore-genesis related remanence, suggesting that the dyke Intrusions
occurred either prior to or at the same time as the mineralisation.
A F.-related remanence (NM2) was found in isolated localities only, and appears to
represent a minor overprinting event in this region with little impact on the
previously-formed ore bodies. Where it co-exists with the NMI component
(Orebody 25), this component appears as a lower-temperature component carried
either by fine-grained hematite/martite, or by maghemite, whereas the NMI
component appears as the most stable component carried by martite. The NM2
remanence is directed northwesterly, shallow upward. Cenozoic overprints, due
to either weathering or viscous origin, have also been found in some localities.
Mt Whaleback Mine
Amongst a total of 53 samples collected from the Mt Whaleback Mine, 34 were from
martite-microplaty hematite ore, and 19 from either non-mineralised BIFs, or shales
interbedded with the ore. Sites MNO 1 (mostly ore), MN04 (ore), MN09 (mostly ore), and

a. Magnetic characteristics
Apart from the Brunos Band BIF and red shale samples, in which magnetite is present,
and the black shales that contain pyrrhotite, magnetic remanence in the rest of the
samples is almost entirely carried by hematite (including martite) (Fig. 6.1, NM09d).
Though a small low-unblocking temperature component is present in some M-(mpl h)
are samples (Fig. 6.1), they are mostly poorly resolved.

Fig, 6,1 Typical demagnetisation curve of Mt Whaleback martite-microplaty
hematite ore. The changes in remanent intensity during stepwise thermal
demagnetisation (demagnetisation steps shown as 'C) are shown in (a), The rapid
drops in intensity between 625'C and 675'C suggest hematite/martite as the
magnetic remanence carrier. The relative rate of intensity changes during the
demagnetisation process is demonstrated by the height of the shaded bars. The
orthogonal plot in (b) demonstrates the changes in both remanence intensity and
direction during the demagnetisation process (also see Fig. 4,9). Filled dots are
projections of remanence after each demagnetisation step on the horizontal plane [as
defined by axes N(orth), East, S(outh), and West], and open circles are projections on
the vertical plane defined by axes West, Up, East and Down (i.e., and east-west
vertical plane). The same convention is followed in all the demagnetisation diagrams,
with the only possible difference being that the vertical plane in the orthogonal plots
can also be a north-south vertical plane.

### page_110
b. Remanence over F. structures
The most convincing F. structures we have sampled are the isoclinal fold at the Bench
22 of western Central Pit (Site NM04, ore, Fig. 6.2), and the overturned fold in Brunos
Band at the eastern side of the Breakthrough (site NMOS & 06, BIF, Fig. 6.3). All three
sites give a stable remanence direction moderately downward toward the south before
structural correction, but the directions become scattered after bedding-correction (Fig.
6.4). This demonstrates that the remanence was acquired after the F. folding.
c. Remanence over F.Jolds
The best meso scopic F. fold in the Whale back mine is the one developed in the M t
Sylvia BIF at the southern wall of Bench 13 (site NM02). It is a refolded F. structure
(Fig. 6. Sa). The characteristic remanence is carried by hematite, either as a single
component (Fig. 6.Sb), or as an intermediate unblocking-temperature component (Fig.
6.Sc). Structural correction of the F. folding makes the remanent directions more
scattered (precision parameter K decreases from 2S.1 to IS.7, and u. increases from
5
13.6° to 17.S0) (Figs 6.Sd and 6.Se). A correlation fold test suggests that remanence was
not acquired before the F. folding, but could have been acquired after about 80% of the
F. folding. This remanence is thus most likely a late- or post-F. overprint. The in-situ
direction is D = 288.So, 1= -30.4°, K = 2S.1, U.5 = 13.6° (the best grouping acquired after
20% unfolding gives D = 286.2°, I = -30.1°, K = 26.2, U.5 = 13.3°).
The other possible F./F. fold is found in the mineralised Dales Gorge Member(?) in the
western Pit. Though the mean direction of the two sites (NM07 and NM08) becomes
closer after bedding correction, the within-site grouping for NM08 becomes worse after
the correction (Fig. 6.6). After comparison with the remanent directions of sites like
NM04 which has no apparent F. or F. modification, and the F.-related remanence
direction (NM02), we interpret the remanence of these two sites as possibly pre-F./F.
origin. The scattering in site NM08 directions could indicate the undetected presence of
F. structural component in that site.
d. Remanence over F.Jolds
Eight samples were collected over a broad F. fold in the ore body at Bench 23 of Central
Pit (Fig. 6.7a). A positive fold test (unfolding increases K from 10.0 to 22.4, and
decrease u. from 18.4° to 12.0°) implies that the remanence was acquired before F.
5
folding.

e. Remanence from the shale units
Five samples were collected from the shale unit in the M-(mpl h)-mineralised Dales
Gorge Member at Bench 21 of Central East Pit (part of site NM01), with two from black
shales, and three from red shales. AF and thermal demagnetisation show that the
remanence in the black shales is carried by pyrrhotite, whereas in the red shales
mostly by hematite. Though mostly poorly defined, the five samples give a mean
characteristic remanence direction of D = 345.6, I = -66.3, u.s = 13.3° in the present
geographic coordinates, which becomes scattered (u.s increases to 44.5°) after bedding
correction for F •. This remanence was probably acquired after the Late Cretaceous (see
more discussion in section 6.7).

f Summary of magnetic remanence results from the Mt Whaleback Mine
The dominant magnetic remanence in the Mt Whaleback Mine (component NM1) is
directed moderately to steeply downward toward the southwest (Fig. 6.8). It was
acquired after F folding, but before F. and possibly before F NM 1 is almost the only
2 3•
remanence vector recorded in the martite-microplaty hematite ores. Martite, a form of
104

### page_119
hematite, is the product of low-temperature oxidation of magnetite, and cannot be
remagnetised without going through recrystallisation (into rnicroplaty hematite), or
being heated up to a temperature close to the Curie temperature of hematite (-675'C),
of which there is no evidence in the study region. It is thus most likely that remanence
NM 1 represents the geomagnetic field at the time of the formation of both martite and
microplaty-hematite, and thus the formation of the Mt Whaleback ore body.
A northwesterly-upward direction (component NM2) has been found in the BIF layers of
an Fa structure. It could have been acquired either during the late stage of, or after, the
Fa deformation, and is interpreted to post-date the Mt Whaleback microplaty hematite
ore formation. Its isolated occurrence implies that F3 deformation had little influence in
the Mt Whale back ore body.
A steep-upward remanent direction is found in shale bands. It is most likely a chemical
or viscous remanence acquired during the Late Cretaceous or later.
Ore bodies 23 and 25
a. Ore Body 23
Eight samples were collected from two sites in Ore Body 23: site OB23-1 was from the
contact zone of a -10 m-wide dyke, which strikes between WNW and NE, and site
OB23-2 was from overturned and isoclinally F 2-folded BIFs, partially M-(mpl h)
mineralised, about 20 m in strike distance westward from the dyke. The purpose of
these samples was to test the significance of the dyke intrusions for the mineralisation.
Whereas the remanence-carrying minerals in the four samples from OB23-1 varies from
hematite-dominant (Fig. 6.9a) to magnetite-dominant (Fig. 6.9b), there is no apparent
difference in the remanence directions carried by the two mineral types (Fig. 6.9b). The
overall mean direction is D = 333.9', I = 59.3', u's = 33.5' (Fig. 6.9c).
Remanence at site OB23-2, on the other hand, was dominantly carried by
hematite/martite (Fig. 6.10a), and it was apparently acquired after the F2 folding (Fig.
6.10b). It is intriguing to notice that the u.s circle of the site-mean direction (D =
286.6', I = 47.4', u.s = 18.0', Fig. 6.10b) largely overlaps with that of site OB23-1 (Fig.
6.9c). This implies that, irrespective of whether the dyke intrusions had played any role
in the mineralisation, they acquired their magnetisation at roughly the same time as the
mineralisation (Li et al., 1993). The magnetisation could have been acquired either

during or after dyke intrusion. It is unlikely to have been acquired significantly before

b. Ore Body 25
Twenty-two samples were collected from five sites around Ore 80dy 25: 15 from martite
goethite ores (sites 0825-1, 0825-2 and 0825-5 - Fig. 6.11a), and seven from Dales
Gorge 8lFs (0825-3 and 0825-4). The major structure is a F2 anticline overturned and
107

### page_122
verging to the north. K-T studies show that the dominant magnetic carriers in fresh ore
samples are martite (hematite). and possibly some maghemite, whereas goethite exists
mainly in the weathered BIFs.
Three remanence components recognised from the other four sites have been found: a
dominant, most stable, and steep-downward component (A) carried by martite, a NW
shallow component (B) possibly carried by maghemite, and a Recent, weathering-related
overprint (C) (Figs 6.11 b-d).
The meso scopic folding at OB25-5 is open and box-like, with broadly upright axial
surfaces. It is developed on the overturned limb of the large-scale F. anticline, which
has minor parasitic folds developed just south of the figured fold. The F. parasitic folds
are tight, overturned and have an axial-surface slaty cleavage which is either sub
parallel to bedding or has a shallower attitude than bedding on this overturned fold
limb. The box-like folds have a more brittle, open fold style than F. and are
incongruous with their being parasitic on the large-stale F.. Moreover, their fold axis
plunges 03° to 071°, oblique to the regional lOOO-trend of F. in this place. Similar
upright box-folds on the bench below the site of OB25-5 have fold hinges trending
toward 120°.
As shown in Figures 6.12a and 6.12b, a simple structural correction (disregarding the
overall overturned stratigraphy) makes the OB25A component from site OB25-5 much
more scattered, whereas the in-situ site-mean directions group quite well (Table 6.1 and
Fig. 6.12c). We thus conclude that component OB25A, which is always carried by
martite and likely represents the ore-forming event there, was acquired after the
wrinkling of the bedding at the site. The overall mean direction of D = 260.6°, I = 69.2°
with N = 4, U9S = 21.5° agrees well with the NMI component from the Mt Whaleback
Mine. Li (this study) prefers to interpret the box-like folds as part of the late stages of
the F. generation, and thus putting the magnetic remanence observed here the same as
the NMI component from the Mt Whaleback Mine, i.e., post-F, but pre-F3 and F •.
However, Powell and Ronaszeki (this study) prefer to interpret differently. They
examined the site twice, once when the palaeomagentic samples were being collected in
1987, and again in 1998, when it was known that the steep southwestward component
of magnetisation overprinted the folds. Site 0825-5 had been removed by mining
between 1997 and 1998, but refolding relationships were found on the bench
immediately below (Fig. 6.11h). Powell and Ronaszeki concluded that the folds are
younger than F., and belonged either to F3 or F •. They therefore argue for a post-F3/F.
age for the observed remanence. However, there is no direct evidence for the correlation

### page_128
b. Martite-microplaty hematite ore in the Boolgeeda Iron Formation
Site BI06 revealed a post-F.(?) remanence (Fig. 6.13) carried by martite/hematite, and
possibly some maghemite. The in-situ directions agree with that of component NM 1.
c. Weeli WoW BIF
Site WW05 was collected from a small ridge. The enormously high Q values and the
scattered remanent directions suggest that this site has suffered from lightning strikes.
d. Joffre Member BIF
Four sites were collected from the Joffre BIF Member in the region: two (JFO I and JF02)
from the Ophthalmia Gorge - 6 km due north of the Newman town, one (JF03) from a
series of small overturned F 2 folds (Fig. 6.14a) in Gorge 5W, -3 km west of Mt Newman,
and one (JF04) from the core of a meso scopic upright F. fold in the Ando's Gorge. Sites
JFOI and JF02 revealed a NW-directed sub-horizontal direction (Figs 6.14b and 6.14c).
Although we are unable to perform a conclusive fold test, the similarity of the in-situ
remanence directions with that of NM2 component suggests that they were probably Fa
related overprints. However, both site JF03 and JF04 give a negative fold test (Figs
6.l4d - 6.l4g), demonstrating a post-F. origin of the remanence. Their in-situ directions
are closely aligned with the NM I direction.
A low unblocking-temperature (S; 300°C) component was identified from site JF04 with a
mean direction of 0 = 18.0°, I = -71.5° (n = 5, ex gS = 22.5°). It is interpreted as a
viscous/weathering overprint acquired during the Cenozoic.
e. Dales Gorge Member BIF
All four Dales Gorge sites (OGOI-OG04) revealed northwesterly, shallow-downward
remanence directions before bedding-correction (See OG04 in Fig. 6.15).
Magnetite/maghemite and hematite carried the same direction. Sub-vertical to
overturned bedding is common in all four sites, which all are on the northern limbs of
large F. folds. Two of the sites are on the overturned northern limb of the Mt Newman
anticline (OGO I and OG03, southern part of Cathedral Gorge), one on the northern limb
of the next anticline to the south (OG04), and the fourth site is on the northern limb of
a regional anticline east of Newman (OG02, Andos Gorge).

The in situ remanence direction from these sites is similar to the remanence in OB23-2.
The bedding-corrected directions are more scattered (a.s increased from 23.7" to 34.1"),

3.
significance. A factor which could have affected the remanent directions is the magnetic

### page_132
f Contact of a northeasterly-trending dyke in Marra Mamba BlF (MM06)
Three out of the four samples revealed a very poorly grouped, steep-downward
remanence direction. The dyke trends northeasterly, and extends about 10 km as
shown on the 1:100 000 Newman sheet geological map (Fig. 4.1). It cuts the F.
structures. Though poorly grouped, the similarity of the mean direction to that of
component NM 1 again suggests the possible synchroneity of the dyke intrusion and the
major regional iron mineralisation. However, according to Powell, the NE-trending dyke
also cuts F3 folds (e.g. -1 km east of Cathedral Gorge) further along strike. If this is
true, this remanence direction, though very poorly grouped here, could be younger than
F deformation. Further investigation of the relationship between these dykes and
3
magnetisation is warranted.

### page_133
6.2 WEST ANGELAS - AREA C REGION (Table 6.2; Fig. 4.2)
Summary
The West Angelas - Area C region is characterised by dominant E-W trending,
mainly F. folds, and the development of martite-goethite ore deposits. Sixty-one
oriented samples were collected from surface outcrops, and five core-segments
from an oriented 60 mm-diameter diamond core in Deposit A of Robe River Mining
Associates deposit at West Angelas.
Like the Newman region, this region also underwent two major remagnetisation
events: a dominant post-F. chemical/thermal event that resulted in the formation
of M-I(g)) ores (goethite is mostly Tertiary voids fills), and a younger overprint
event which totally reset the magnetic signature in carbonate rocks, but is also
recorded by finer-grained martite/hematite. The earlier event has a mean
remanent direction of D = 222.4' , 1 = 70.7' (N = 3, ag. = 19.3'). The corresponding
= =
palaeomagnetic pole (WAC1) falls at (45.2',265.5') with DP 29.1", DM 33.5',
which is, within 95% confidence, the same as the direction of magnetisation in
the microplaty hematite ore at Mt Whale back. The younger overprint component
has a mean direction ofD = 313.7' I = -31.8' IN = 3, a •• = 14.6'" which agrees with
the late to post-F 3-related overprint component found in the Newman region.
Although this younger event is more prominent in the West Angelas - Area C
region than in the Newman region, it is still a much weaker overprint event
compared with the older one. The corresponding palaeomagnetic pole (WAC2)
= =
falls at (-46.3', 207.6') with DP 9.2', DM 16.4'. No samples of oriented core
were available from the West Angelas martite-goethite mineralisation, so that the
question of whether that mineralisation was formed at the same time as the
magnetisation in the immediately underlying magnetite-rich BIF is left as an open
question.
West Angelas and The Governor
a. Surface M-g-((g-(()) )) ore in the Mt Newman Member of the Marra Mamba BIF
Nine samples were collected from three sites (WAOI - WA03) at the eastern end of the
martite-goethite Deposit A. Although samples were distributed across the nose of the
syncline, they failed to reveal any consistent remanent direction due to lightning strikes
119

### page_134
and surface weathering. K-T analysis and demagnetisation results suggest that both
maghemite and martite (hematite) exist in these samples.
b. Marra Mamba BIF samples from industrial diamond 60 mm core WAA 992
Five samples were collected between core-depths of 120.79 m and 133.49 m: two from
the Mt Newman Member, and three from the MacLeod Member. These samples come
from the zone immediately below the martite-goethite orebody. Ten specimens were re
cored from these core segments. Whereas the iron-rich specimens, dominated by
magnetite, have very strong susceptibility and remanence, specimens from low-iron
intervals have susceptibilities below 100 x 10.5 SI. A low-temperature (up to 450° C;
Fig. 6.16a) component revealed a NM2-like direction (0 = 320.7°, I = -33.5°, n = 6, u.s =
19.9°) after tilt-correction to orient specimens in relation to the drill-core, with mixed
polarities (Fig. 6.16b). A fold test is not possible because all samples were from one
limb; the direction in stratigraphic coordinates is 0 = 327.7°, I = _8.9° with u.s = 19.9°.
A higher-temperature component is present in four of the specimens (e.g. Fig. 16.6a),
but the directions are scattered.
c. Wittenoom Formation
Fifteen samples were collected from two sites in the northwestern foothills of The
Governor. Two components are clearly separated from these samples: a viscous
component sub-parallel with present geomagnetic field direction (component Co in Fig.
6.17a), and a characteristic northwesterly-upward direction (component CI in Fig.
6.17a). As shown in Figure 6.17b, the directions from the two sites group well before
bedding correction, but diverge after bedding correction. The gentle folding of the
bedding is likely to be part of F 2, and the site means are better clustered in situ than
after unfolding. This suggests that the magnetisation is younger than the folding. The
close alignment of the in-situ directions with the NM2 direction (Table 6.1) suggests that
the remanence was most likely due to the same thermal/chemical event near the end
of, or younger than Fo. The remanence is likely to be carried by magnetite.
d. Mt Sylvia and Brockman BIFs
Four samples were collected from the Mt Sylvia BIF ridge, halfway down on the western
slope of The Governor. All samples showed moderate to high susceptibility, high
anisotropy, and extremely high (mostly >20 A/m) remanence, with three of the four

### page_138
samples having remanence sub-parallel to the bedding. This site is regarded as of no

Two sites were collected from the Dales Gorge (WA04 and WAOS) on the southern side of
the Coondawanna Ridge. WA04 was from a cave developed inside a -Sm amplitude F2
anticline (Fig. 6.18a). A stable remanence, carried mostly by hematite and with dual
polarities, gives an in-situ mean direction of 0 = 231.2°, I = 77.7° (n = 6, lX.s = 35.9°).
Bedding-correction scatters the directions from individual samples (Fig. 6.18b-c), and
thus suggests a post-F. origin for the remanence. Note that three of the samples have
an anisotropy of between 1.3 and 1.5. However, the conclusion remains even if these
samples are excluded.
Site WAOS was from a metre-scale parasitic F. syncline -20 m downstream from WA04
(Fig.6.19a). A steep-downward direction, carried by both magnetite and hematite, has
been revealed (Fig. 6.19b). A clear negative fold test (Fig. 6. 19c-d) suggests a post-F.
origin for the remanence.
Mining Area C
Four sites were sampled from natural outcrops in BHP's mining Area C. One was from
the M-G ore Deposit B (site AC02), and one from Deposit C (site ACO I), both of which
are in the Marra Mamba Formation. The other two sites were from Brunos Band (site
AC04) and Dales Gorge Member BIFs (site AC03), both on the eastern side of the Tucker
Box Gorge. All sites are on the northern limb of the broad, E-W trending Weeli Wolli
anticline (Fig. 4.2), along which numerous M-G deposits have been found. Sites AC03
and AC04 cover small F. structures which enabled fold tests on the remanence.
Sites ACOI and AC02 showed similar demagnetisation behaviour, and are combined in
data analysis. Two characteristic remanences have been identified: a steep-downward
remanence carried by martite (hematite), and a northwesterly, shallow-upward direction
carried by maghemite/magnetite and very fine-grained martite/hematite (Fig. 6.20).
Goethite clearly exists in some samples and carries a recent geomagnetic field direction.
A fold test on the steep-downward direction (Fig. 6.20c) demonstrates that it was post
folding. A fold test is not available for the NW shallow-upward direction.
Site AC03 revealed two similar components, although the steep-downward component is
more dominant and has higher unblocking temperature (Fig. 6.21). Martite/hematite
124

### page_139
are again the main magnetic minerals. A negative fold test indicates that both
components were acquired after the F2 deformation. Site AC04 from Brunos Band failed
to reveal any consistent remanence direction.

### page_144
6.3 TOM PRICE MINE AND THE TURNER SYNCLINE (Table 6.3; Fig. 4.3)
Summary
Compared with the Newman region, the Tom Price Mine, and the Turner Syncline
in general, is characterised by a more widespread late to post-F. overprint which
is directed northwesterly upward (or the opposite polarity), and a more restricted
occurrence of the post·F. (but pre·F.?), southwesterly steep·downward overprint
direction. Another interesting observation is that samples of M·(mpl h) ore at the
contact of a NW-trending dyke (TP07) give remanence directions close to the late
to post-F. related overprinting direction. It implies that either the dyke intruded
at about the same time as the F. deformation, or much of the Tom Price ore body
had undergone a pervasive chemical/thermal overprint during or after the F.
deformation. There is also the possibility of a ca. 755 Ma overprint component
found in some localities inside the Tom Price Mine. Due to the interference
between F. and F. in the Tom Price Mine, correct restoration of the pre-F.
remanence direction is not always possible.
Tom Price Mine
Twenty oriented samples were collected from martite-microplaty hematite lump ore
within the open cut of the Tom Price Mine. In addition, 14 samples previously collected
from the open cut, with eight from the ore, and six from a red shale unit, were also
analysed during this project. The results are discussed below.
Structures in the pit are complex. F. trends more easterly than the southeasterly
trending F which is parallel to the southern Batter fault. Many of the minor folds in
3,
the pit and on the access roads to the tailings area northwest of the mine are minor F.
folds. In the main' pit, these F. folds deform the low-angle lag faults. The situation is
further complicated by the presence of northwesterly-trending dolerite dykes, some of
which act as discrete margins to the ore, and others of which appear to include
fragments of mineralised BIF. Structural relationships indicate that the ore post-dates
F., and that the NW-trending dykes were emplaced around the time of mineralisation.
The low-angle normal faults, which could have formed in the same extensional event as
the emplacement of the mafic dykes, are folded by F •.

1991, was from the north wall of Bench 705, SE Prong, with seven samples from the

### page_148
Dales Gorge ore, and six from interbedded red shales. The bedding tilts dominantly
toward the NE, with dip angles of ca. 40 ± 10' (Fig. 6.23a). Apart from three M-(mpl h)
ore samples which give northerly-downward remanent directions, the majority of the
samples from both the ore and red shales give a southwesterly, steep-downward
direction (Fig. 6.23b). Bedding correction does little to change the grouping of the
directions. The in-situ site-mean direction is remarkably similar to the post-F. NMI
direction from Mt Whale back. Although the bedding-strike corresponds to F. fold axes
directions, it is not possible to work out the exact contribution of F. and F. to the
bedding attitude. Site TP08 consists of two samples collected from a vertically-dipping,
M-(mpl h)-mineralised Brunos Band at the western wall of Bench 765, SE Prong (Fig.
6.24a). The two samples give an in-situ direction of D = 16.0', I = 35.6'. A full bedding
correction would bring the mean direction into D = 210.8', I = 56.0' (Fig. 6.24b). Its
bedding-corrected direction is similar to the NM 1 direction. This can be accommodated
if the folding was mostly F. and the magnetisation was acquired before F •.
Alternatively, since the in-situ direction falls close to the remanence obtained from the
755 ±3 Ma Mundine Well dyke swarm in western Pilbara (Wingate and Giddings, 1999),
this remanence could be the result of similar NE-trending dyke intrusions in this
region.
Site TP04 from Dales Gorge ore at the southern wall of Bench 690, SE Prong, gives a
well-grouped, NNW, shallow-downward direction (Fig. 25). The bedding-corrected
direction is similar to the inferred late to post-F. remanence direction (component NM2)
from Mt Whaleback.
Site TP07 is from iron ore at the southern contact zone of a -15 m wide, NW-trending
dyke (Fig. 6.26a) at the western wall of Bench 765, SE Prong. All samples are within 15
m of the dyke, with samples C to E at the contact. Four samples give westerly-upward
directions, whereas one has a southeasterly direction (Fig. 6.26b). Bedding correction
makes the directions slightly better grouped with a shallower inclination (Fig. 6.26c).
Note that both the in-situ and bedding-corrected directions are close to the inferred late
to post-F. remanence direction (component NM3) from Mt Whaleback.
Sites TP03 (ore at northeastern Bench 690, SE Prong; n = 4), TP05 (ore at contact of
NW-trending dyke, Bench 765, SE Prong; n = 3) and TP06 (ore at southwestern Bench
765, SE Prong; n = 6) all revealed north to northwesterly directions, but without within
site consistency (Fig. 6.27). Like the case for site TP08, the in-situ northernly-downward
remanence direction in site TP03 could also be due to the ca. 755 Ma dyke activities.

Turner Syncline - natural outcrops
A systematic sampling program was carried out on natural outcrops of the Turner
Syncline. The palaeomagnetic results are discussed in ascending stratigraphic order.
a. Marra Mamba Formation
Three sites were collected from this BIF formation: one (MMOl) from the southern limb
of western Turner Syncline, and two (MM04 and MM05) from the northeastern limb
close to Tom Price (Fig. 4.3). A Recent-field component carried by goethite, and a mostly
steep-downward component carried by both magnetitefmaghemite and
martite/hematite (Fig. 6.28a-b) have been revealed from sites MMOI and MM04 (Fig.
6.28c). whereas only the Recent-field component has been found in site MM05. The in-

### page_155
situ directions are similar to the NM 1 direction. Bedding correction makes the two site
mean directions close to antipolar, and the fold test is thus inconclusive.
b. Wittenoom Formation
A successful negative fold test was performed on a metre-scale E-W trending upright
fold close to the technical office complex of Hamersley Iron at Tom Price (Li et al. 1993).
Seventeen more samples from three sites (WD02 to WD04) were collected during this
project from folded dolomite on a roadside about 3 km south of Mt Nameless (Fig. 4.3).
Apart from a small viscous component, thermal demagnetisation revealed a dominant
NW-upward direction (Fig. 6.29a-b). Thermal and AF demagnetisation behaviour of the
samples (Fig. 6.29a-b) suggests that both magnetite and pyrrhotite are present in the
dolomite. Like the early results, the new results again provide a negative fold test (Fig.
6.29c-d), suggesting a post-F3 folding origin.
c. Mt Syluia Formation
Three sites (MF02-04) were collected from the Mt Sylvia BIF at the southern foothill of
Mt Nameless (Fig. 4.3). Sites MF02 and MF03 were from small, NW-trending folds,
suspected to be F3 (Figs 6.30a, 6.3la).
Site MF02 revealed a poorly-resolved, poorly-grouped, moderate to steep downward
direction, which became more scattered after bedding-correction (Fig. 6.30b and d).
Although this may be seen as indicating a post-folding origin for the remanence, the
poor data quality does not warrant such an interpretation.
Site MF03 revealed a poorly grouped, northwesterly shallow-inclined remanent direction
carried by both magnetite and hematite. Bedding-correction makes the grouping even
poorer (Fig. 6.3la). A component similar to that found in site MF02 is seen in sample
MF03C only, and was carried by hematite (Fig. 6.3lb). Site MF04 has probably been
subject to lightning strike, and failed to reveal any consistent direction.
d. Brockman Iron Formation
One site was collected from each limb of the western Turner Syncline (Fig. 4.3). A
characteristic remanence was revealed at high temperature steps only in site BMO 1 (Fig.
6.32a), and at a broader temperature spectrum in site BM07 (Fig. 6.32b). The two sites
are roughly antipolar before bedding correction, and less so after the correction

### page_160
(Fig. 6.32c). The ex for the overall mean of the two sites increases from 21.4° in-situ to
95
33.8° after the bedding correction. This suggests a post-folding origin for the
remanence. Note that the in-situ directions are similar to the overprint direction in the
Wittenoom Formation and other late to post-F. overprint directions.
Two samples were collected from a small F, ductile fold in the Joffre BIF member, south
of the West Pit Road in western Tom Price Mine (Figs 4.3 and 6.33). A negative fold test
suggests a post-F. origin for the remanence. Their in-situ mean direction of D = 330.9°,
1= 41.3° is different from the other inferred pre-F directions (e.g. NM1). This could be
3
due to the local F. refolding, which is visible from a distance. Detailed structural
mapping in that region is needed before the effect of F. deformation on the remanence
direction can be corrected.
e. Weeli Wolli Formation
Two sites were sampled across the syncline (Fig. 4.3). Both sites contain magnetite, and
were variably affected by lightning strike. Site WWO I failed to reveal any consistent
remanent direction. Site WW02 revealed a northerly downward direction after AF
demagnetisation eliminated the effect of lightning strikes (Fig. 6.34). Though no fold
test is possible, the in-situ mean direction is closer to the NMl remanent direction than
the bedding-corrected one. A NM2 direction is found in one of the five samples from the
site, which is regarded as an outlier when calculating the site-mean direction.
f Boolgeeda Iron Formation
The two sites from the Boolgeeda Iron Formation (B104 and BIOS in Fig. 4.3) revealed
excellent NM2 directions (-16.8° to 321.4°, and -30.3° to 317.9°, respectively) which
pass a negative fold test (Fig. 6.3Sb-c). The remanence is dominantly carried by
hematite (Fig. 6.35a).
g. Other sites around the Turner Syncline
Two sites were collected from the Fortescue Group basaltic units along the Tom Price -
Paraburdoo road: one from the Pyradie Formation (PP01), and the other from the
Boongal Formation (BG01) (Fig. 4.3). These rocks retain a very weak magnetic
remanence carried by magnetite, with an in-situ direction of either northwesterly
upward, or its reversed polarity (Fig. 6.36). Since only two samples from BGOI retained
the stable remanence, they are combined with PPO 1 in data analysis. This in-situ
146

### page_161
direction agrees with the regional late to post-F 3 overprint direction. The (l.s of the
overall mean increases from 14.9" to 18.5" after bedding correction, indicating a
possible post-deformational origin.
Six samples were collected from a NW-trending dolerite dyke in the Rocklea Dome (sites
RDO 1 and RD02 in Fig. 4.3). Unfortunately they failed to retain any characteristic
remanent direction.

### page_166
6.4 PARABURDOO REGION (Table 6.4; Fig. 4.4)
Summary
The general characteristics of the remanent magnetisation In the Paraburdoo
Channar region are very similar to those of the Tom Price region. The west
southwesterly, steep-downward direction was found from one locality in the hard
cap M-(mpl h) ore In Bench 11,18 East of the Paraburdoo Mine, and two Fortescue
Group basaltic outcrops outside the mine. However, there is a possibility that the
remanence from the Fortescue Group Is of primary origin (see discussion in
section 6.7). On the other hand, post-F., northwesterly shallow-inclined directions
(late or post-F,?) have been found in M-(mpl h) ores of both the Paraburdoo and
Channar Mines, in baked zones of the northwesterly-trending dykes, and in a
number of outcrops outside the mines. Where the two components coexist and
both are carried by magnetite, the second component occurs as the lower
temperature one, suggesting a possibly younger aged thermal overprint. A
shallow, north-south trending remanence was found from baked rocks of a
younger, NE-trending dyke exposed in the Channar Mine. The orientation of the
dyke, as well as its remanent direction, suggests that it probably belongs to the
755 ± 3 Ma Mundine Well dyke swarm.
Because of the wide occurrence of dolerite dykes in the Paraburdoo-Channar region,
along with normal sampling targets, contact zones of the dykes have been paid special
attention in this region. Most of the dykes trend northwesterly, but there is a ca. 40-50
m wide, NNE-trending dyke at the Channar Mine which is believed to be younger than
the NW-trending ones. This dyke has been correlated with the Mundine Dyke swarm by
Tyler (1990).
Paraburdoo Mine
Samples were collected from three sites in the Paraburdoo Mine: PDO 1 from weathered
M-(pll h) ore at Bench 11, 18 East of the Paraburdoo Mine, PD02 from M-(pll h) lump
ore at Bench 14, 4 East east, and site PD03 from contact zones of NW-trending dykes at
Bench 14, 4 West. Their results are discussed below.
a. PD01: M-(mp/ h) hard cap ore at Bench 11, 18 East
Among the four samples collected, two contain significant amounts of goethite with no

c. PD03: M-(mpl h) ore and contact zone oja NW-trending dyke, Bench J5 , 4 West
PD03A was collected from M-{mpl h) ore -2m below a l.5m-wide wavy dyke at the
western end of Bench 15,4 West. It revealed a northwesterly-upward remanent direction
carried dominantly by magnetite, but also by martitelhematite (Fig. 6.37b). Samples
PD03B and PD03C were collected from BIF within two metres of the chilled margin of a
NW-trending dyke. Both samples revealed a shallowly-inclined remanence direction
trending to the SE (Fig. 6.37d). Like sample PD03A, both magnetite and hematite give
the same remanent direction.
Channar Mine
Among the four sites collected from the Channar Mine, three were related to the main
NE-trending dyke (CM 01, 03 and 04), and CM02 was from both BIF adjacent to a NW
trending dyke (samples A and B), and Martite-microplaty hematite ore (samples C to E).
a. CM02: martite-microplaty hematite ore
The sampling site is located in a microplaty hematite ore body (Channar Main Deposit),
located in a 60 m to 100 m space between two NW-trending dykes. Whereas three ore
samples away from the dyke give NW-trending remanent directions (Fig. 6.31a & b), one
sample from a secondary ore "dyke" along the contact zone of the dyke gives a southerly
directed remanence, also carried by martitelhematite (B in Fig. 6.38b). The NW-trending
population becomes more scattered upon bedding correction (F2 structure?), and the
direction is similar to the regional late to post-F) overprint direction. The sample B
direction, on the other hand, is parallel to the direction revealed from the NE-trending
dyke at Channar (see section below), and the thin ore "dyke" is therefore regarded as of
possible hydrothermal origin related to the NE-trending dyke intrusion.
h. CMO J, 03 and 04: sites related to the main NE-trending dyke
Among the three sites, both CM02 and CM03 are from the eastern contact of the main
dyke at natural outcrops, and CM04 is from metre-scale BIF inclusions within the dyke

### page_172
exposed at a roadcut. Because the dyke is too weathered for magnetic study, the
fresher baked country rocks, and the baked BIF inclusions, were sampled to reveal the
palaeomagnetic characteristics of the dyke.
Magnetite dominates the magnetic remanence in all three sites. There is some erratic
behaviour in site CM03, and some samples in site CMOI (Fig. 6.39a), during low-field
demagnetisation. Such erratic remanence is probably due to lightning strikes. Site
CM03 failed to reveal a consistent remanence direction. However, both of the remaining
two sites carry a north-south trending, subhorizontal remanence (Fig. 6.39b-c). The
presence of dual polarity suggests that the cooling of the baked rocks lasted long
enough to average out the secular variations. The corresponding palaeomagnetic pole
(NED) falls close to the 755 ± 3 Ma Mundine Well dyke swarm in western Pilbara
(Wingate and Giddings, 1999), which suggests that this local dyke is probably part of
the same dyke swarm, confirming a conclusion reached earlier by Tyler (1990).
Outcrops outside the mines
a. Bunjinah Formation of the Fortescue Group
Two sites were collected from the Bunjinah Formation: one (BJOI) from Palm Spring,
about 22 km NNE from Paraburdoo, and one (BJ02) along the Paraburdoo-Tom Price
highway (Fig. 4.4). Magnetite is the dominant magnetic carrier in both sites (Fig. 6.40a
& b). However, their remanent directions are quite different. Whereas BJO I carries a
northwesterly upward direction similar to the regional late to post-F. overprint direction
(Fig. 6.40c), BJ02 gives a steep-downward direction which is close to the post-F.
remanence direction prominent in eastern Hamersley (Fig. 6.40d). As will be further
discussed in sections 6.7, this remanence may be of primary origin.
b. Jeerinah Formation of the Fortescue Group, main entrance of the Paraburdoo Mine
Three components have been identified from one site (JROl) collected from the roadcut
outside the main entrance to the Paraburdoo Mine. After the removal of a viscous
Recent-field component (CI) by about 250·C to 300·C, an intermediate-temperature
component (C2, up to 500·C) and a higher-temperature component (C3, ca. 550·C) are
revealed (Fig. 6.41). C2 is subparallel to the regional shallow NW-directed, late to post
F. overprint direction. Although the C3 direction is closer to the dominant post-F. steep
remanence direction found in the Newman region, the possibility of it being a primary
remanence can not be ruled out (see section 6.7).

c. Ma"a Mamba Fonnation, gully east of Mt Paraburdoo
Six samples were collected from a cherty dolomite unit around a metre-scale E-W

### page_178
6.5 DUCK CREEK REGION (Table 6.5; Fig. 4.5)
Summary
Magnetic remanence in the Duck Creek region is characterised by the total
absence of the post·F2 ' steep·downward remanence direction which dominates the
eastern Hamersley Province. Instead, the remanence is mostly directed towar'd
west-northwest, with shallow inclinations. Although the possibility of some rocks
still retaining their primary remanence can not be totally ruled out, the overall
distribution of the remanent directions from the region becomes more scattered
by correcting the F3 structure (Fig. 6.44), suggesting a late or post-F3 origin for
them. They most likely to represent a thermal/chemical event during the late
stages of the ca. 1,700 Ma Ashburton Orogeny. Surface samples from the Barrett
Lennard deposit [(M-(mpl HI conglomerate ore], as well as an individual M·(mpl HI
ore pebble, give, the same remanence direction. This suggests that a post·
depositional mineralisation process, possibly related to the Ashburton Orogeny,
totally reset the magnetic record in the deposit, including that of any pre-existing
mineralised pebble.

Whereas small east-west trending folds, possibly belonging to F., are seen in outcrop
near the southeastern core of the Duck Creek syncline (Wright, 1996), the major
regional structures in the Duck Creek region are believed to be F._ No post-F. steep
down southwesterly remanence, like the dominant magnetic remanence in the
Newman-West Angelas-Area C regions, has been found in the Duck Creek area.
Instead, the majority of the samples from the Duck Creek region carry a west to
northwesterly trending, shallowly-inclined remanence, possibly related to the late stages
of F deformation. They are discussed below in ascending stratigraphic order_

a. Dales Gorge and Weeli Wolli BIFs
One site was collected from each formation. Three of the four samples from site BM02
give a westerly downward direction carried by magnetite (Fig. 6.45a). The in-situ
direction is very similar to those found in the Dales Gorge BIFs in the Newman region
(Table 6.1). Although the significance of this direction is as yet unclear, it may be a
combination of the two major overprint components. Site WW06 reveals a poorly
grouped remanence direction before bedding correction (Fig. 6.45b), which is typical of
the ?late or post- F overprint directions found in the central and eastern Hamersley
3
Province. The remanence is carried by both magnetite and hematite.
b. Woongarra Rhyolite
Two sites were collected from the Woongarra Rhyolite, both from the northern limb of
the Duck Creek Syncline. Well-grouped remanent directions have been revealed from
both sites, with magnetite being the carrier (Fig. 6.46a). Because these remanent
directions are closely aligned with the bedding strikes, they change little by bedding
correction (Fig. 6.46b-c). A McFadden (1990) correlation fold test (definition one)

indicate that the remanence is more likely to be of post-folding origin (95% critical value

c. Boolgeeda Iron Fonnation
Twenty-three samples were collected from three sites along the same section as the two
Woongarra Rhyolite sites. The samples were from red and grey siltstone layers, with
either magnetite or hematite being the magnetic carriers (Fig. 6.47a-c). Like the
situation with the Woongarra Rhyolite results, bedding correction makes little difference
in the overall mean direction (Fig. 6.47d-e), and a McFadden (1990) fold test gives no
inference as to whether the remanence is pre- or post-folding. Both sets of data are
listed in Table 6.5.
d. Turee Creek Dolomite
Two sites were collected. Samples A to D of site TK02 were taken from a metre-scale
fold, possibly F in the regionally southwesterly-dipping structure. Site TKO 1 revealed
2,
a late Cenozoic overprint direction with both normal (carried by magnetite) and reversed
(carried by hematite) polarities (Fig. 6.48a). Samples A-D from site TK02 reveal a
northwesterly, shallow-upward direction carried by magnetite, which becomes scattered
after bedding correction (Fig. 6.48b-c). The remainder of the samples from that site
failed to reveal any consistent remanence direction.
e. Mt McGrath Fonnation (Barrett-Lennard Deposit)
Six samples were collected from the Barrett-Lennard Deposit. Despite all the samples
containing both pebbles and matrix, they all show a stable, northwesterly-trending
remanence direction carried by martite/hematite (Fig. 6.49a-c). Thin section
observations show that microplaty hematite is abundant in both the pebbles and the
matrix (see descriptions of samples MGOIA3 and MGOIF3 in Appendix one), and the
margins of the ore pebbles are in many places obscured by dissolution and/ or hematite
recrystallisation (Fig. 6.49d). A hematite pebble with the dimension of 23 mm x IS mm
x 4 mm was extracted from the block sample of MGOIB, and subjected to stepwise
thermal demagnetisation. The result is almost identical to that of the whole rock (Fig.
6.49a, b). This demonstrates that the M-(mpl H) pebble and the recrystallised
microplaty hematite in the matrix were both formed during the same event (i.e. any pre-

f Cheela Springs Basalt
Two sites were collected from the basal units of the Cheela Springs Basalt (Fig. 4.4).
Site CBOI was from basaltic units with a NW strike, which reveals a magnetite-carried

direction agrees with the in-situ remanence directions found in majority of the samples
from the Duck Creek region (Fig. 6.44a).

A and B coming from one limb of a small E-W trending anticline (F2; Wright, 1996), and
the rest from flatter-lying beds. A NW-trending remanence, carried by both magnetite
and hematite, is found from this site, and becomes scattered after bedding-correction
(Fig. 6.51a-c). If the small fold belongs to F2 as suggested by its E-W trend, this
remanence must have been acquired after F2 deformation. Like site CBO 1, the in-situ
direction of CB02 is also in general agreement with the rest of sampling sites from the
Duck Creek region (Fig. 6.44a).
g. Duck Creek Dolomite
Among the two sampling sites, site 0001 revealed a SE-upward remanence direction
(Fig. 6.52a-b) of unclear origin and geological significance. Two samples from site 0002
carry a direction similar to the shallow northwestward overprint directions (Fig. 6.52c &
e), and the rest revealed a late Cenozoic direction carried by both magnetite/maghemite
(both normal and reversed polarities) and hematite (reversed polarity) (Fig. 6.52d-e).

### page_191
6.6 HAMERSLEY - CHICHESTER RANGES REGION (Table 6.6; Fig. 4.6)
Summary
The major aim of studying the less-deformed northern Hamersley province was to
examine the regional extent of various magnetic overprinting events. Among the
20 sampling sites collected from the region, covering both the Fortescue and
Hamersley Groups, we found the northwesterly, shallow-upward overprint
direction to be widespread, reaching as far north as the Chichester Range. On the
other hand, steep-downward remanent directions were found in two sites only:
one from the Jeerinah Formation at the Tom Price-Marandoo road, and the other
from the Tumbiana Formation of middle Fortescue Group in the Chichester
Range. This component, carried by magnetite with unblocking temperature close
to 580'C, can either be a F.-related overprint, or alternatively, a primary
remanence (see section 6.7).
The sampling localities in this region are shown in Figure 4.6, and the magnetic
remanence results are listed in Table 6.6. One site each from the Kuruna Siltstone
Member of the Fortescue Group (site KSOI), the Mt McRae Shale unit in the Bee Gorge
(site MSOI), and the Weeli Wolli Formation (WW03) failed to reveal any consistent
remanence direction apart from Recent field overprint due to weathering. One site each
from the Marra Mamba Formation (MM03), the Mount Sylvia Formation (MF06) and the
Weeli Wolli Formation (WW04) failed to reveal any consistent remanence direction.
These sites will not be discussed further. Results from the other rock formations are
discussed below in an ascending stratigraphic order.
a. Tumbiana Fonnation, Fortescue Group, Chichester Range
Three sites (TMOI-03) were collected from the fiat-lying, volcaniclastic Tumbiana
Formation of the Fortescue Group along the roadsides of the Great Northern Highway
that cuts across the Chichester Range (Fig. 4.6). Although the Tumbiana Formation is
close to the base of the Fortescue Group in the Chichester Range, it falls in the middle
Fortescue Group in more complete successions in the northern Pilbara.
Whereas site TM02 failed to reveal any stable remanence, site TMO I revealed two
remanence components after the removal of a viscous component: an intermediate
temperature (l00-450°C), northwesterly shallow-upward remanence direction (el), and

southern part of the Hamersley Province (although it is closer to the NM 1 direction). As
further discussed in section 6.7, this component could be a primary remanence.
Site TM03 is stratigraphically the highest among the three sites. Four out of the six
samples reveal an east-westerly, sub-horizontal remanence direction (Fig. 6.53d).
Although this direction is closer to that of the C 1 component than the C2 component
from site TMO I, it does fall on the great circle containing the two components, and its
unblocking temperature is often higher than that of C 1. This site has been excluded
from the regional mean-calculation because it may represent a combination of Cl and
C2.
b. Maddina Basalt, Fortescue Group, Chichester Range
Six samples were collected from the Maddina Basalt, Fortescue Group, southern
Chichester Range (site MBMO 1 in Fig. 4.6). Five of the samples revealed a north
westerly, shallow-upward direction (Fig. 6.54). A temperature of ca. 450' C is normally
sufficient to clean this component, but it was not possible to reveal the higher-

### page_196
temperature component. Like C1 from site TM01, this remanence is interpreted as a

c. Jeerinah Formation, Fortescue Group
One site (JR02) was collected from flat-lying basalts on the roadcut of the Tom Price
Marandoo road (Fig. 4.6). Half of the ten samples failed to reveal any consistent
remanent direction, and AF demagnetisation was shown to be ineffective in isolating
magnetic components. However, thermal demagnetisation has revealed three discreet
components: a viscous recent-field component (C1), an intermediate-temperature (300-
500°C) component (C2) directed northwesterly and shallow upward, and a higher
temperature component (C3) that behaves as a stable endpoint at the 500-580°C steps
(Fig. 6.55). In three samples all three components can be identified (e.g. Fig. 6.55b),
and magnetite is the carrier mineral for all components. C2 is sub-parallel to the
widespread regional late to post-F3 overprint, and the ineffectiveness of AF
demagnetisation in delineating the components suggests that it is likely to be a thermal
overprint. C3 is either an F,-related overprint, or a primary remanence (see further
discussion in section 6.7).
d. Wittenoom Formation
Five sites were collected from the Wittenoom Formation in this region (sites WD07 to
WDll, Fig. 4.6). Apart from variance in their bedding attitudes, site WD08 from the
Harnersley Gorge has a strong axial-plane cleavage (dips 69° to 207°), and a local fold
axis trending 305-315°. They are suspected of being F. structures.
Apart from site WD09, which revealed a weathering-produced Recent remanence only,
all the other four sites reveal a northwesterly, shallow-upward remanence direction (Fig.
6.56). Like other sites from this formation, the remanence is very well defined, with a
maximum unblocking temperature of between 450° C and 525° C. The fact that the
cleaved rocks (site WD08) give the same remanence as the non-cleaved rocks suggest a
negative "fabric test" (Li et al., 1988), and therefore a late to post-cleavage origin. The
negative regional fold test (Fig. 6.56g) also suggests that the remanence could not be
older than the NW-trending deformation, i.e., late to post-F

e. Dales Gorge Member of the Brockman Iron Formation

### page_201
6.7 SUMMARY AND DISCUSSION
Four, possibly five, phases of remanent magnetisation have been identified from the
Hamersley Province (Table 6.7):
(I) A post-F" pre-F. (possibly also pre-F3) magnetic overprint (NMI or HPI) is pervasive
in the Newman, West Angelas and Area C regions, less prominent in the Tom Price and
Paraburdoo regions, and totally lacking in the western (Duck Creek region) and
northern (Hamersley and Chichester Ranges) Hamersley Province (Fig. 6.58a). It is
commonly carried by hematite/martite, but sometimes also by magnetite and
maghemite. It is believed to be of thermal/chemical (mostly chemical) origin.
Fold tests suggest that the NM I/HPI remanence was recorded after the F, deformation,
but before the F. folding observed in the Mt Whaleback Mine. If F3 and F. are of similar
age, this would place the NM I / HP I mineralisation event between the F. and F 3
deformations. A pre-F3 age for this remanence is further supported by the behaviour of
the F3-related regional overprint. Firstly, because the NM I /HPI phase of magnetic
overprint is related to iron mineral oxidation/recrystallisation caused by ore fluids of
low to intermediate temperature (Powell et al., 1999), and that carbonate rocks, which
normally record the latest regional thermal/chemical magnetic overprint, retained the
F3-related NM2/HP2 remanence only, we argue that the NMI/HPI remanence is older
than the NM2/HP2 remanence, thus pre-F.. Secondly, the NMI/HPI remanence
always occurs as the most stable magnetic component when coexisting with the
NM2/HP2 remanence. The age of the remanence is thus regarded as toward the end of
the Ophthalmia Orogeny, e.g. ca. 2200 Ma, which is the same time as the emplacement
of the Cheela Springs Basalt (Martin et al., 1998).
There is, however, some doubt about the age of this magnetisation component, largely
due to the difficulties in interpreting some refolding structures in Orebody 25. At site
OB25-5, the NM I/HPI remanence postdates minor refolding of F. structures. Although
Li (this study) prefers to interpret such minor refolding as possibly of late-F. age, thus
agreeing with the regional palaeomagnetic interpretations, Powell and Ronaszeki (this
study) considered the refolding as either F 3 or F. because the fold trend (066°) is close to
the F 4 trend in the Whaleback Mine. They would thus regard the remanence to be post
F3 in age, i.e. younger than ca. 1700 Ma. There are also difficulties in separating F. and
F3 structures in some sites in the Tom Price area. Further palaeomagnetic
investigations need to be undertaken in places where the age of the folding is better
constrained.

Note that the regional overall mean directions neglect the geographic spread of the
sampling sites. A95 = half angle of the 95% confidence cone of a palaeopole.
(2) A late to post-F. magnetic overprint (NM2 or HP2) that is widespread in the western,
central and northern Hamersley Province, but less prominent in the eastern Hamersley
Province (Fig. 6.58b). It can be carried by either magnetite or hematite/martite, and in
some places by maghemite. Where it coexists with the previously-mentioned component
(or possibly a primary remanence, see discussion about component 3), it always occurs
as the lower-temperature component. It appears to be of mostly chemical origin in iron
ores and BIFs, of thermal/chemical origin in carbonate (in which this overprint is
pervasive), and mostly thermal origin in massive volcanic rocks. The temperature which
caused the thermal overprint in some of the volcanic rocks is estimated to be ca. 250 ±
100°C according to the Middleton and Schmidt's (1982) theoretical T-t chart. On the
basis that (1) the remanent direction agrees with the syn-folding remanence reported by
Schmidt and Embleton (1985) from the Mt Jope Volvanics around the Rocklea Dome, (2)
the lack of any pervasive deformation in the region after the Ashburton Orogeny, and (3)
the possible late-F. origin suggested by the fold test results of site NM02, we consider
the remanence to be related to the late stage of the F deformation, i.e. the Ashburton
3
Orogeny, with an age of ca. 1700 Ma. We note, however, that the age of F. is
unconstrained by stratigraphy, and the age of the remanence could thus be younger
than 1700 Ma. Possible ages could be ca. 1600 Ma during the early stage of the
opening of the Bangemall Basin, or ca. 1000 Ma when the Bangemall Basin was folded.
Figure 6.59a plots the palaeopoles corresponding to the two dominant remanences in
the Hamersley Province. The smallest dots represent poles based on less than three
sampling sites, the intermediate-sized dots represent poles from at least three sites, and
the large grey dots are province-wide mean poles of the two phases of remagnetisation
(Table 6.7). Poles from each phase of magnetisation, those from the younger phase in
particular, are reasonably well-grouped, with overlapping 95% confidence "ellipsoids".
However, the two populations are clearly distinct.

### page_208
Figure 6.59c plots the new poles (Table 6.7) together with existing Archaean to
Palaeoproterozoic poles from the Pilbara craton (Table 6.8). The palaeopole previously
obtained by Porath and Chamalaun (1968) from the Whaleback hematite ores (pole
NMA) falls between the HP1 and HP2 pole populations, but close to pole OB23 from Ore
Body 23. The Porath and Chamalaun (1968) results have not been corrected for post-F,
structure, which could be the reason for the difference between their pole and NM 1 pole
of this study. On the other hand, palaeopoles reported by Schmidt and Clark (1994),
including the poles from the Tom Price and Paraburdoo ores (poles TPA and PBA in Fig.
6.58c), the fiat-lying Dales Gorge and Joffre BIFs at Wittenoom (pole WBl), the BlF
samples at Paraburdoo (pole FBI' from in-situ direction, and FBI after bedding
correction), and the syn-folding overprint pole JO from the Mt Jope Volcanics, fall into
the HP2 population. We therefore confirm the interpretation of Li et al. (1993) that
much of the Hamersley, the central, north and western regions in particular, has
undergone a phase of pervasive magnetic overprint, most likely during the late stage of
Ashburton Orogeny at ca. 1700 Ma.
(3) A possible primary remanence from four sampling sites in the little-deformed
Fortescue Group volcaniclastic rocks (Fig. 6.58c). As shown in Figure 6.60, the four
Fortescue Group site-mean directions group better after the bedding correction, and
therefore pass a regional fold test (the geographic spread of these sites is ignored here).
A,s of the average pole position reduces from 64.3° in-situ to 32.7° after bedding
correction of two of the sites, whereas the other two sites are fiat-lying. Assuming the
tilting of sites BJ02 and JR01(both in Fig. 4.4) was due to the F. deformation, such a
positive fold test would suggest a pre-F and possibly primary, origin for the
2,
remanence. Figure 6.59c shows that the corresponding palaeopole (FG) agrees with
previous poles from the Fortescue Group (poles RB and JV) and similar-aged dykes
(poles BR and CD) (Table 6.8).
However, given the small number of sites available, the large errors associated with two
of the sites and the mean pole position (Fig. 6.59b and Table 6.7), and the uncertainty
whether all the bedding tilting in the sampling sites (mostly very gentle) is of F. origin,
the interpretation and reliability of this remanence should be treated with extreme
caution.
It should be noted here that the Archaean to Palaeoproterozoic apparent polar wander
path (APWP) for the Pilbara craton, combining poles obtained during this study (Table
6.7) and existing results (Table 6.8), is not unique. This is partly due to the inherent
polarity ambiguity carried by any palaeomagnetic remanence, and partly due to the

7. TIMING AND GENESIS OF IRON ORE MINERALISATION
- FROM A PALAEOMAGNETIC PERSPECTIVE
7.1 TIMING OF THE IRON ORE FORMATION EVENTS
As shown in section 6, (?)Cretaceous to Recent magnetic components are prominent in
only a few severely weathered shale units. They are present in carbonate rocks and
BIFs only as the most unstable component (lowermost temperature or demagnetisation
field), possibly of weathering or viscous remanence origin. They are rarely noticeable in
both M-(mpl h) and M-((g)) type iron ores, where either martite and/or microplaty
hematite are the dominant iron minerals. We therefore conclude that none of the M·
(mpl h) and M·((g)) deposits we studied were formed during the Cretaceous
Cenozoic period despite there being goethite void infJ.!ls in ores close to the Tertiary
weathering surface. We note that the friable M-G ores, which have -50% goethite, were
not studied in this project, and could have formed in the Cretaceous-Tertiary interval.
All the ores we studied, with the exception of the small pocket of magnetite ore next to a
ca. 755 Ma dyke in the Channar Mine, are dominantly composed of microplaty hematite
and/ or martite, which can only be thermally remagnetised by heating to a temperature
well over 600'C. However, fluid inclusion analysis (Powell et aI., 1999) coupled with the
general greenschist or lower grade of metamorphism in the underlying mafic Fortescue
Volcanics (Smith et aI., 1982), indicates that the maximum temperature the ores have
been subjected to is below 400'C. We therefore take the magnetic remanence carried
by hematite/martite in the ores as representing the remanence they acquired
either during the ore formation, and/ or during subsequent recrystallisation.
We see no difference in the magnetic remanence directions carried by either
martite or microplaty hematite in the M·(mpl h) deposits (the Mt Whaleback, Tom
Price, Channar and Paraburdoo deposits). It is even more intriguing to note that
the same dominant remanence (NMI or BPI) found in the Mt Whaleback deposit
also dominates in the M·G or M·(()) deposits in the region (Orebodies 23 and 25,
and deposits in the Area C region). We therefore have no reason to believe that
the martite and microplaty hematite in at least the studied deposits in the
Newman and Area C regions were not formed at a similar time interval.
Our results presented in Chapter 6 (see Table 6.7 and Figs 6.58 - 6.59) suggest that
there are two major phases of Precambrian remagnetisation in the Harnersley Province
199

### page_214
in-situ iron deposits. They therefore reflect two phases of martite/hematite
formation (thus ore-formation) or recrystallisation:
• The first is the NMl/HPl phase, most likely of late Ophthalmian (ca_ 2200 Ma?)
age or soon after_ It is found dominantly in the eastern Hamersley Province
(the Mt Whaleback Mine. Ore Bodies 23 and 25, and Area e), but also had
impact in the central Hamersley Province (the Tom Price and Paraburdoo
deposits). However, there is no sign of its occurrence in the western Hamersley
Province. The ore types can be either M-(mpl h) deposits (the Mt Whaleback,
Tom Price and Paraburdoo deposits). or M-ll )) / M-G deposits (Orebodies 23 and
e
25, and deposits in the Area region). The early M-(mpl h) ore bodies probably
provided the detrital microplaty hematite clasts found in the Lower Wyloo Group
(Martin et al., 1999) and the Mount McGrath Formation (Morris, 1980). This phase
of ore genesis occurred when the Pilbara was at a palaeolatitude of ca. 40·.
• The second is the NM2/HP2 phase, likely related to (but mostly after) F.
deformation (ca. 1700 Ma). It is strongest in the western (Barrett-Lennard
deposit) and central (Tom Price, Paraburdoo and Channar deposits) Hamersley
Province, but had little impact on the deposits in the east Hamersley Province
e
(Mt Whaleback, Ore Bodies 23 and 25 and Area deposits). Like the geographic
relationship between the NMI/HPI phase of magnetisation and the F2 deformation,
the regional distribution and intensity of the NM2/HP2 phase is also in general
accordance with that of the Fs deformation. We thus argue that the significance of
the NM2/HP2 mineralisation event decreases toward the east. In regions with strong
impact from both events, record of the younger one would dominate. We thus see a
mixed, but dominantly the younger, magnetic record in the central Hamersley
deposits. This second phase of ore genesis occurred when the Pilbara was in the
tropics.
Even if some of the alternative ages for the two phases of mineralisation are taken
(e.g., if NM2/HP2 is ca. 1700 Ma and NMI/HPI is ca. 1600-1550 Mal. they still
remain Proterozoic. In the unlikely possibility that NM 1 / HP i is as young as 1600-
1550 Ma, there must have been an older mineralising event between 2400-2200 Ma
to account for the detrital grains/clasts of microplaty hematite reported by Goode
(1981, p. 121) and Martin et al. (1998) from the Beasley River Quartzite in the lower
Wyloo Group, and by Morris (1980) from the unconformably overlying Mt McGrath
Formation.
200

### page_215
7.2 ORE GENESIS DISCUSSION: A CASE FOR A HYPOGENE MODEL?
Despite its simplicity and popularity, the following observations are incompatible with
the supergene model (e.g., Morris, 1987) for the in-situ M-(mpl h) or M-G [commonly M-((
)) or M-((g)) in this study; Table 4.1 and Appendix 1) deposits in the Hamersley Province:
1. Results of this study indicate that mineralisation is related to widespread thermal
chemical events. Magnetic overprints related to the second major mineralisation event
(ca. 1700 Ma?) spread as far north as the Chichester Range. Such widespread thermal
chemical events can be readily explained by tectonic/thermal fluids flows related either
to orogenic and/or magmatic activity (see discussions in section 2.2; Fig. 7.1). On the
other hand, the supergene model has difficulties in explaining why the thermal
chemical overprint is found remote from the mineralised zones in the non-BIF rocks in
the northern Hamersley Province .
. 2. There is no magnetic evidence for Mesozoic/Tertiary supergene-enriched in-situ iron
deposits. Instead, palaeomagnetic results suggest that both the M-(mpl h) ores (e.g., Mt
Whaleback), and the M-((g)) or M-(( )) ores in the eastern Hamersley Province (Orebody
25 and Area C deposits) were also formed during the MNI/HPI mineralisation event.
Microplaty-hematite and martite probably represent different levels of oxidation and
recrystallisation, yet they may coexist in the same deposit (e.g. Harmsworth et al., 1990)
because of small variations in the physical-chemical conditions. The relatively small
amount of goethite (in comparison with microplaty-hematite or martite) in the studied
deposits (Table 5.17) formed mostly during Mesozoic to Recent weathering (see
Appendix I).
3. The presence of large hematite crystals in the matrix of hematite conglomerate in
both the Barrett-Lennard deposit and in the basal Wyloo Group (Martin et aI., 1999)
clearly suggests a hypogene origin. The fact that the hematite pebbles in the Barrett
Lennard deposit carry the same remanence as the hematite in the matrix suggests that
the hematite in those pebbles were also recrystallised during the hydrothermal process.
Zones of very coarse microplaty hematite have also been found in the Channar Main
deposit (see thin-section description of sample CM02E in Appendix 1). Samples from
both the Barrett-Lennard deposit and site CM02 carry a single-component NM2/HP2
remanence, therefore they are unlikely to be related to younger events.
4. The identification of hematite ore pebbles from basal Beasley River Quartzite (Goode,
1981; Martin et al., 1999) means that microplaty-hematite ores already existed and
201

### page_216
were uplifted during the Ophthalmia Orogeny (Fig. 2.2). This leaves little time for the
supergene enrichment to occur, and provides no mechanism for any supergene
enriched martite-goethite ores formed at the erosion surface below the Beasley River
Quartzite (Morris, 1985, 1987) to go through the burial metamorphism process to be
converted into microplaty-hematite ores.
5. The temporal and spatial relationship between the mineralisation and orogenic
events, and the elevated (200'C to 400'C) temperature of mineralisation fluids involved
(Powell et al., 1999), are more consistent with a hypogene ore genesis. High
temperature mineralisation events have also been reported by other researchers from
the Tom Price deposit (Geology Department, Hamersley Iron Pty. Ltd. et al., 1998).
Our efforts of trying to examine the timing relationship between the mafic dyke
intrusions and the M-(mpl h) ore genesis did not achieve unequivocal results.
Remanence from the contact zones of a NW-trending dyke in Orebody 23 agrees with
this ore-genesis related remanence, which suggests that either the dyke intrusions
occurred prior to the HPI mineralisation but subsequently remagnetised by the
mineralisation event, or they intruded at the same time of mineralisation. Similar
conclusions also apply to the situations in Tom Price Mine and Paraburdoo regarding to
the HP2 mineralisation event and NW-trending dykes.
Structural and palaeomagnetic evidence available is consistent with the micro platy
hematite ores being generated in the same time interval, or after, intrusion of the NW
trending dykes. The chemistry of these dykes has not yet been investigated, as most of
the exposures available are weathered to clay. However, structural evidence that the
dykes intrude all formations up to, but not higher than, the Cheela Springs Basalt
suggests that the dykes could be feeders to this continental flood basalt (Dow et al.,
1997), which is dated ca. 2,200 Ma (Martin et al., 1998).
One major difficulty the hypogene model has in the Hamersley Province deposits is the
lack of a source for the large amount of oxygen that was required for oxidising the
magnetite in the BIFs into hematite. Figure 2.10 presents an hybrid ore genesis model
for the martite and microplaty-hematite deposits in the Province (after Powell et al.,
1999). It involves the mixture of both hot basinal fluids and cooler meteoric fluids
driven from the uplifted mountain belt into the foreland basin. The meteoric fluids
provided the crucial oxygen needed to oxidise the original magnetite in the BIFs into
martite/hematite. The major difference between this model, and the model shown in
Figure 2.9 (Li et al., 1996), is that in this model all fluids are flowing toward the craton,
202

### page_217
and a source for oxygen has been clearly identified. The model is basically a hypogene
one with elements (Le. the involvement of meteoric fluids) from the supergene model.
Such an ore genesis model maybe applicable to both phases of mineralisation identified
in this study. However, because of the lack of any good age constraint for the NW
trending dykes in the region, we are as yet uncertain as to whether they played any role
in elevating the 'geothermal gradient and thus driving the fluid circulation.

### page_223
Appendix one: Ore-type classification by Dr R C Morris on polished
thin-sections cut from ore samples
February 22'· and March 17'" 1999.
Preliminary note.
I have been asked to classify the specimens listed below using the shorthand
terminology developed for the 1976 - 1995 CSIRO-AMlRA iron are program, and
described originally in Morris, R. C. (1985). Genesis of iron ore in banded iron-formation
by a supergene and supergene-metamorphic process - a conceptual model, in Handbook
of Strata-Bound and Stratiform Ore Deposits. (Ed. K H Wolj). Vol. 13, pp 73-235 (Elsevier:
Amsterdam).
A revised version of my original terminology together with explanatory notes, is
attached.
Polished thin sections were used for this examination following a cursory glance at the
original specimens. I have made no effort to classify the samples using the PIOC hand
specimen system. I was informed that the thin sections had been prepared from cored
specimens used for the paleo-magnetic analyses, and it was immediately apparent that
some of the sections had been cut parallel or sub-parallel to the bedding thus severely
limiting the value of the thin section for diagnostic purposes. The thin sections were all
well polished but for the most part were too thick to allow light to penetrate through
goethite or indeed in places through quartz, defeating the purpose of using polished thin
sections rather than polished blocks. /Note by authors of the MERIWA242 report: Those
unsatisfactory thin-sections have since been remade and redescribed by Dr Morris again
on March 1 7 1999; See the last section of this appendix!.
Shorthand terminology /from Morris (in preparation), after Morris, 1985}
A "shorthand" terminology for petrographic description of ores has been introduced to
simplify communication in iron ore geology. It is used extensively in the Hamersley
iron ore industry.
Despite their relatively simple mineralogy, BIF- derived ores may be texturally very
complex. This complexity results chiefly from the multitude of different bands of the
original rock, each of which could give rise to several different textural variants in ore.
Petrographic descriptions of these ores can be difficult to follow. The shorthand version
simply classifies the mineralogical components of the ores on the basis of their
derivation.
The BIF -derived bedded ores consist of two basic "elements" :
- the derivatives and residuals (ie. martite, kenomagnetite, primary hematite) of the
primary iron oxides and,
- the goethite-replaced matrix or its dehydrated or metamorphosed equivalent.
The shorthand nomenclature uses upper or lower case letters as symbols to represent
major or lesser components, respectively, in a one, two, or three term label (sometimes a
fourth term is needed, taken from the third group in the Table) which specifies the
mineralogy, the textural features, the metamorphic state and, by implication, though
independent of it, the genetic history of the ore.

BIF·derived bedded ores. (Note that upper case and lower case
