The first term of the label is used for the derivatives or residuals of the primary oxides,
magnetite and primary hematite; these include:-
- Km or km. for kenomagnetite (oxidised spinel phases between magnetite and
maghemitel and,
- M or m for martite (hematite pseudomorphs after magnetite). which for convenience
also includes primary hematite, though this could be shown separately as H or h;
The second term refers to the replaced BIF matrix, ie. goethite, G or g. as in M-G or M
g. Where secondary minerals have formed by dehydration or metamorphism (ie. not as
void filling). from the initial enrichment-goethite, appropriate symbols are enclosed in a
single set of brackets, ( I. Thus, (G>BI or (g>hl refers to fine-grained hematite after
goethite, almost always a dehydration product due to "weathering". In contrast, (mpl HI
refers to metamorphically generated microplaty hematite (so-called ·specularite"). Note
that both primary mpl B. found as residuals in ore, as well as the extremely fine (Imp!
H)) found as drusy encrustations in weathering voids, are identified in the label by the
absence of brackets in the first case, and by double brackets in the second. Secondary
magnetite, typically associated with contact metamorphism is shown as (Mtl.
210

### page_225
The third term relates to leaching within the matrix goethite. Residual goethite from
leaching is typically ochreous (oG or ogl Voids formed by leaching are shown as double
brackets II II, but this term is often left out, though implied by the presence of leaching
residues, as in M-oG.
Addition of tertiary components into the voids can be indicated by convenient symbols
within the brackets, ego ((qtzll or new goethite ((Gil. For example M-g-((sil/kaoll
represents an unmetamorphosed martite-rich sample with a goethite replaced matrix,
partly leached, with the resultant voids containing silica and kaolinite. M-llsil/kaoll
indicates that all the initial goethite has been leached, and the voids filled by silica and
kaolinite. In this case, the second term g is no longer valid.
The terms are separated by dashes, ego M-g (ie. martite goethite) is a simple
unmetamorphosed supergene-enriched sample with clearly identifiable pseudomorphs
of ex-magnetite and gangue minerals. Subdivisions of terms are separated by slashes,
as in m/km/h-(hl-g, which is an unmetamorphosed, martite, m, kenomagnetite, km,
primary hematite, h, ore, in which the goethite replaced gangue has been partly
dehydrated to fine grained hematite (hI, leaving some residual supergene goethite, g.
A metamorphosed ore where martite is a major component, where microplaty hematite
has grown from the goethite and, where some of the residual goethite has been leached
out, is shown as M-(mpl HI -g -1111 A major derivation of this type is M-(mpl HI-II II,
where the complete leaching of the residual goethite results in premium grade, low
phosphorus, pure hematite ore with moderate porosity (a desirable attribute for direct
lump furnace feedl. This is usually written as M-(mpl HI for convenience, though
strictly the term actually implies a metamorphic ore in which all the initial goethite was
converted to microplaty hematite.
The system can be made more quantitative by adding digits to the symbols in
proportion to the mineral composition, either totalling 10 or as a percentage:-
ego 7M-3G; SOM-20(mpl HI-30g; leaching of the latter gives SOM-20(mpl HI, in which
30% porosity is implied.
A highly leached ore with partly filled voids could be shown as:-
40M-30(HI-301l10Sill or 4M-3(HI-3111Sill, which indicates 30% voids, ie. (()I, with 10
of the 30 filled by silica, and 20 still as voids.
A few additional words or sentences could be added to supplement the description.
Subscript tenninology (used particularly in photomicrographs)
G" Goo G q, G km, and G~trix respectively indicate goethite pseudomorphous after silicate,
carbonate, quartz, kenomagnetite and matrix in general.
(H,), {H,I, {Hql, (Hkml, and (l:\".tnx) respectively represent hematite formed by dehydration
of goethite pseudomorphs after silicate, carbonate, quartz, kenomagnetite, and matrix
in general.

Shorthand classification of 20 iron ore/enriched BIF specimens from
examination of polished thin sections.
OB 23 02D3
Enriched BIF including stress quartz, with mpl H of uncertain origin, some possibly of
primary BIF origin. Could be classified as oxidised BIF + M-mpl h. Remnant "chert" is
coarse grained.
OB 23 02 B2
Similar to D3 but with more normal "chert" rather than stress quartz.
NM 01 J2
M - (mpl h)
NM 07 Bl
Classic textured M - (mpl h)
NM 08 C2A
M - (mpl h) - g>h
A heavily leached specimen with only very minor g> h, but this material indicates
dehydration due to relatively close-surface effects.
NM 09 Gl
Classic M - (mpl h) ore with some good core textures in the martites.
TP 03 B2
Coarse M - (mpl h) ore with classic mpl h texture
TPOSAI
M / m>km - (mpl h) ore, ie. typical M - (mpl h) ore with specks of newly developed - not
remnant, kenomagnetite in some of the martite.
TP07 E2
M / m>km - (mpl h) ore with more obvious, though still trace amounts of secondary
kenomagnetite. More importantly, kenomagnetite is present in rare grains of mpl h,
proof positive that the km is a later formed product due to reduction in the system. I
have described similar but much greater effects from the Southern Batter ore at Tom
Price where the effect is associated with high levels of secondary apatite and minor
pyrite among other components.

Complex textures due to weathering.

PO 02 C3
M - (mpl h) - (( G - (( ))))
The internal double bracket implies much reworking by repeated solution and
reprecipitation of g, and the effects in the specimen are clearly surface related.
It is unlikely there is any residual primary (recrystallised) g, but the thin section is
possibly not cut perpendicular to the bedding.
PO 03A2
Finely banded, very porous M - (mpl H) - (( ))
The mpl H shows an unusual variation in grain size which may be due to two different
mechanisms. First, it may be due to the presence of some primary mpl h, not
uncommon in Paraburdoo BIF, or it may be that a second finer generation of mpl h
formed due to a post ore intrusion similar to that at Channar. A single TS cannot be
used to clarify this situation. I am not aware of any post ore dykes except at Channar
and Barrett Lennard, so this would be an interesting study. Note however that the
sample does not show any other features of recrystallisation that is typical of the ore
along the dyke contact at Channar (see Morris, 1985).

### page_228
A very "reworked" hard cap sample with evidence of repeated solution and precipitation
of goethite. The g > h material includes a form of extremely fine mpl h that is clearly
related to weathering and not the typical metamorphic type. Similar micro mpl h is
seen in most carapace/hardcap zones but is not found in the ore proper, indicating its
superficial origin.
AC 02 B2
M-((g>h))
This is an example of a carapace ore ie., an M - G ore in which near surface
dissolution/reprecipitation of goethite has been followed by dehydration of the goethite
to hematite. I could see no evidence of original carbonate or silicate textures.
AC 03A2
M/h - G type ore but now M/h - (( g/h )) - (( g > h))
Clearly a near surface specimen. The sample contains both primary hematite which is
rare in these northerly Marra Mamba ores as well as layers of secondary hematite
layered with the goethite in places.
The inference from this information is that there are three different generations of
hematite present.
WA 03A2
M - g - (( g -(( )) ))
A typical complex textured product of weathering within the hydrated zone of the hard
cap which penetrates to considerable depths along the Area C range. Only minor
remnants of poorly preserved primary ex- carbonate/silicate goethite pseudomorphs
can be found in the general murk of the weathering products.

The following samples were submitted for examination on Monday
15tb March
BI06A
M - (mpl H) - g - Hg , h)) - H ))
This is a classic mpl h texture, finely laminated and resembling Paraburdoo 4E ore, in
having long narrow well defined raft forms(ex-magnetite) with abundant off-shoots of
mpl h. Two types of goethite are present - tertiary infill material due to surficial
processes (also colloform hematite), and a second type, recrystallised goethite, possibly
remnant PreC replacement material.
CM02E
M - (mpl H) -H ))
Very rare goethite is seen as a void filling ie. Hg )).
Note the zone of very coarse mpl H, probably representing a patch of secondarily
recrystallised mpl h, and containing only very rare kenomagnetite and one speck of
pyrite.
This recrystallisation is not comparable to the type of major reworking found along the
Channar intrusive contact, as seen for example in Figure 88 (Morris, 1985. Wolf
Volume) where total destruction of the mpl h texture can be seen. However this radical
alteration fades rapidly away from the contact.
TPOSA
M - (mpl h) - H ))
Only very minor to rare M E kenomagnetite and even rarer mpJ h E keno
TP07E
M - (mpl h) - (m EkE m)
Dominantly irregular martite with patches of small mpl h mainly as off growths. Note
the fairly abundant kenomagnetite with significant re-oxidation to martite. Though
rare, the presence of keno in mpl h grains is a clear indication that the keno is not a
remnant of the original magnetite, and suggests a later (ie. post-ore) event.
NM09G
M - (mpl h) - H ))
Note the zone of very coarse martite and the presence of abundant raft martite showing
the typical Whale back ghost - growth patterns.
MGOI A3
215

### page_230
A fairly typical Barrett-Lennard ore conglomerate composed dominantly of < 1.5 cm
pebbles of M - {mpl H} ore with minimal porosity, and with fine overgrowths of mpl h
growing into the "dirty" matrix of fragmental hematite and chert. The presence of mpl h
in the matrix is interpreted as resulting from recrystallisation of matrix goethite. One
large curved quartz fragment appears to be a recrystallised colloform chalcedony
goethite composite.
MG01 F2
A finer-grained conglomerate {< 0.5 cm} with typical Barrett-Lennard M- {mpl HI
fragments, often well rounded, and, as usual, with new mpl h on the fragment
boundaries or in the matrix.
There is some "recrystallised " goethite often enveloping mpl h. The recrystallisation is
to fan-like aggregates which is not typical of superficial weathering infill. It may be
residual Pree {Precambrian} material, but this is highly conjectural.
The matrix and some of the pebbles contain quartz aggregates which apparently was
derived from chalcedony (the original growth features are still preserved). This is
probably a recent event, similar to that observed in many ore body weathering zones.
See for example Figures 96 and 97 (Morris 1985).
